title: Alief Boards ‘Borges and Me,’ Closes Major Market Theatrical Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:56am PT Alief Boards ‘Borges and Me,’ Closes Major Market Theatrical Sales (EXCLUSIVE) By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna 2 days ago Sanfic Prizes: ‘Monguen’ and ‘Narciso’ Win at Pared-Back Ceremony Due to Sudden Demise of ‘A Fantastic Woman’ Director Sebastián Lelio 3 days ago Seville European Film Festival Honors Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Cartoon Saloon 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Luis Gnecco and Fionn Whitehead in 'Borges and Me' France and U.K.-based Alief has boarded as a sales agent “Borges and Me,” a big scene adaptation of U.S. writer Jay Parini novelized memoir of a life-changing encounter with Argentine literary great Jorge Luis Borges. Directed by Marc Turtletaub (“Jules”) and produced by his label Big Beach (“Miss Sunshine”), “Borges and Me” stars Fionn Whitehead (“Dunkirk”), Luis Gnecco (“Neruda”) and Alan Cumming (“Avengers Doomsday”). Related Stories Sanfic Mórbido Lab Lineup Ranges From an LGBTQ Alien Monster Comedy to a Mapuche Parable, Extreme Horror and Cold War Sci-Fi Alex de la Iglesia on His Upcoming Chilean Shoot ‘The Misunderstanding’: ‘Reality Has Become My Parallel World’ “Delightfully imbued with poetry, magical realism and melancholy, ‘Borges and Me’ is a charming ride with an outstanding British cast. We are delighted to be representing the film,” said Alief President Brett Walker, announcing the pickup. The Edinburgh Festival world premiere has also closed first major market theatrical deals before the AFM with Icon Distribution (U.K. and Ireland), Rialto Distribution (Australia and New Zealand), German-speaking Europe with MFA Film and Spain, bought by Alfa Pictures across what alien describes as “multiple major markets.” Alief is now in conversations with buyers from Central Europe, MENA, Mexico, Cono Sur countries of Argentina, Chile and Uruguay and Asia, it told Variety on the first day of trading at the American Film Market . Written by Oren Moverman (“The Messenger”), working off an earlier adaptation by “Borges and Me” picks up on Parini (Whitehead) in 1971 as young American graduate student at Scotland’s St. Andrews U. desperate to find his voice as a writer, who is persuaded by mentor Scottish poet and Borges translator Alistair Reid, to chauffeur Borges for a week’s road trip in the Scottish Highlands to meet poet George Mackay Brown (Peter Mullan). Their journey—an improbable road trip in an old Morris Minor—transforms from a reluctant obligation into a profound, life-changing experience, Alief noted. In real-life, Argentina’s Jorge Luis Borges was a towering literary presence. Asked to name the greatest works in Latin America literature, Nobel Prize winner Mario Vargas Llosa answered “Borges, everything.” Yet Borges wrote famously in a poem that “I have committed the worst of all sins: I have not been happy.” The Borges Parini encounters in 1971 is a 72-years legend making up for lost time: eager, though blind, to grasp the moment, feel it to its fullest. As played by Gnecco, that drivers moments of comedy, but as the film builds in emotion in his second half, delivers a life changing lesson for Parini. “ Borges has remained with me every day of my life,” he says in his voiceover narrative. “Oren Moverman pivots between moments of graceful poetry and others of simpler feelgood sentiment. The final balance slightly favors the latter,” Guy Lodge wrote in an upbeat Variety review. Peter Mullan (“My Name Is Joe”), Freya Mavor (“My Policeman,” and Morven Christie (“The Bay) also star. “Borges and Me” is a Big Beach presentation of an Ossian International, Big Beach, Lemming Film, and A Private View production. Alex Polunin, Turtletaub, Michael B. Clark, Tim Foley produce; Stephen Burt, Moverman and Parini executive produce. “It is a thrill to work with Big Beach,” added Alief partner Miguel Govea. “Their gorgeously shot ‘Borges And Me brings to life the book, capturing its essence of time, place, and recollection in a strikingly clear and evocative upbeat road movie that audiences and buyers are connecting with.” Director Marc Turtletaub added: “We are thrilled to be working with Alief for international. Their passion for the film was apparent from the first conversations we had with them. And we love the enthusiasm from the distributors who they have partnered with.” “We fell in love with ‘Borges and Me’ for its warmth, gentle wit and endearing charm. It’s a beautiful story about an unlikely friendship between two very different generations, and how much they come to learn from one another,” said Kelly Roger CEO, Rialto Distribution. “We are very excited to be releasing ‘Borges and Me ‘in the U.K. and Ireland next year and can’t wait to share it with audiences everywhere,” said Spencer Pollard, CEO, Icon Film Distribution, a John Gore Studios company “‘Borges and Me’ is a delightful package -– combining the poetic of Borges with the magic of the Highlands. We trust German arthouse audiences will love it,” added Christian Meinke,foinder of MFA Film Distribution. title: Gabriella Yacyk Joins Unicorn As Head Of Comedy
full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Paul Wesley Latest To Join Netflix’s ‘Icebreaker’ ‘Chucky’ Creator Don Mancini Signs With Independent Artist Group Lisa Edelstein, Kevin Pollak & Joe Swanberg Among New Additions To SM Goldberger’s ‘Your Heart Is A Hummingbird’ View All November 11, 2026 8:53am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gabriella Yacyk Matthew Gilbertson EXCLUSIVE: Unicorn , the 360 management firm and content studio, has expanded its executive team with the hiring of Gabriella Yacyk . Yacyk, most recently Senior Director of Development at The Second City, will lead talent management and IP development for Unicorn’s comedy division, reporting directly to co-CEOs Scott Dunn and Chris Gera. “Gabriella is a true comedy industry unicorn, who cut her teeth at some of the most iconic comedy institutions,” Dunn and Gera said. “Welcoming her to our leadership team underscores our desire to identify and foster singular comedic voices, serving as true partners to talent as they work to develop new and exciting content.” Related Stories Late Night TV James Talarico Stuns 'SNL' With Post-Midterms Cameo & "Trump Freezers" Swipe Podcast Comedians Leslie Liao & Jason Cheny Team With All Things Comedy On 'Happy Fun Times' Podcast During her nearly three years at The Second City, the legendary comedy institution that helped launch the careers of everyone from Bill Murray and John Belushi to Tina Fey and Steve Carell, Yacyk spearheaded their expansion into original media for all platforms. She oversaw a slate of scripted and unscripted television, podcasts and digital originals, and launched their first digital comedy ensemble, an initiative focused on developing emerging comedic talent through original short-form content. Watch on Deadline Prior to The Second City, Yacyk held development roles at Comedy Central, where she worked with emerging and established comedians including Bowen Yang, Rachel Sennott, Ayo Edebiri, Benito Skinner, Mary Beth Barone and Stavros Halkias. Her work spanned talent development, original programming and stand-up, including Comedy Central’s Up Next showcase, Comedy Central Stand-Up Presents and hour-long stand-up specials Esther Povitsky: Hot for My Name and Josh Johnson: #(Hashtag) . Based in Gowanus, NY, Unicorn launched in April 2025 under the leadership of creator economy veterans Dunn and Gera. Previously, Dunn co-created popular digital properties Recess Therapy and Bob Does Sports at Doing Things Media, while Gera led digital content strategy at BuzzFeed and Comedy Central. Unicorn’s hiring of Yacyk emphasizes their goal of further expansion into the comedy content realm, both by building long-term infrastructure and support for comedic clients, and developing innovative IP. One recent effort in IP building is the YouTube show Human Trials , hosted by comedian Mark Normand, where comedians perform for hyper-specific live audiences — i.e., 50 bald men, 50 Gen-Z girls or 50 clowns. The show garnered 25 million views in its first week. title: Justin Long, Banks Pierce & Katy Mixon Greer Starring In Family Pic ‘Slater’s Gold’; Producer-Director Launches Texas Studio — AFM
full_text: Skip to main content By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas Britt Robertson Joins Kellan Lutz In Faith-Based Survival Thriller ‘The Rescue’ — AFM Andy Garcia Joins Tim Roth & Timothy Spall In ‘Murdering Michael Malloy’ — AFM May El-Toukhy’s Venice Golden Lion Winner ‘Woman Unknown’ Gets U.S. Deal During AFM View All November 11, 2026 8:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Justin Long, Banks Pierce and Katy Mixon Greer Getty/Courtesy EXCLUSIVE : Justin Long ( Dodgeball ) and Katy Mixon Greer ( American Housewife ) will star with Banks Pierce ( The Pitt ) in family film Slater’s Gold. Also starring are Kate Wilson, Henry Heffernan, Keith Rushing, Brooke Lyons, Harrison C. Thomas, Todd Terry and Glenn Morshower. The film from writer, director and lead producer Micah Lyons ( Bad Men Must Bleed ) recently wrapped production after shooting in Shreveport, Louisiana and will be screening privately for potential buyers and sales agents at this week’s AFM in LA. Related Stories News Matthias Schoenaerts & Diane Kruger Headline 'The Writer', Thriller Set In Underground Graffiti Art World -- AFM News Britt Robertson Joins Kellan Lutz In Faith-Based Survival Thriller 'The Rescue' -- AFM Slater’s Gold “follows 13-year-old Slater (Banks Pierce), as he discovers a mysterious clue linked to lost Civil War gold. Determined to help his impoverished single-mother (Katy Mixon Greer) escape the clutches of her scheming fiancé, Everett (Justin Long), Slater sets out on a dangerous adventure through rural Louisiana swampland with his little brother Noah (Henry Heffernan) and his fearless crush Lindsay (Kate Wilson). Guided by the wisdom of his grandfather (Keith Rushing), Slater must navigate the terrifying town-recluse, unforgiving terrain, a dilapidated salt mine, and find the treasure before it’s too late. But with Everett standing in their way, Slater soon discovers that some things are worth far more than gold.” Watch on Deadline Slater’s Gold , is produced by Breath of Life Productions in association with Bleu Bayou Pictures and Aisle7 Post, with Micah Lyons, Bridget Uhles, J.C. Doler, and Harrison C. Thomas serving as producers. The team also includes Keith Rushing as executive producer and Eric Gibson as line producer. Slater’s Gold creative team includes cinematographer William Hellmuth, casting director Tracy Kilpatrick and music by Erick Schroder. Original story and songs are by Keith Rushing, screenplay is by Micah Lyons. The film marks the launch of Lyons Family Studios, a full-service film and TV studio with three sound stages and an LED Volume headquartered in Longview, Texas. In 2027, Lyons Family Studios and Breath of Life Productions will release Stigmas (in post-production), a romantic thriller starring Amelie Anstett, Robert Knepper, Mia Fugate, Harrison C. Thomas and Leah Kate, and is gearing up to shoot the Latina-driven story of Lost Girl , based on the story of Rebecca Contreras. According to the producers, Lost Girl is financed and currently in the development, packaging and casting phase. Filming is slated for spring 2027 at the Lyons Family Studios. Inspired by his own childhood, writer-director Micah Lyons shared: “I am so proud to be a part of this amazing and heartfelt story. As a child of the 90s, my aim was to make something that felt just like the films I grew up on – equal parts fun, authentic and emotionally rich, highlighting real situations that real kids go through every day across America. As an ode to the classics like Stand By Me and The Sandlot , this is the movie that millennials have been begging Hollywood to make since we were kids!” Justin Long is represented by Independent Artist Group and Yorn Levine. title: Benson Boone Set to Perform at NHL’s 2027 Winter Classic in Salt Lake City (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Singer Benson Boone performs at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival at T-Mobile Arena on Sept. 19, 2026. Kayla DeLaura/WireImage Benson Boone is set to headline the entertainment portion of the National Hockey League’s 2027 Discover Winter Classic, The Hollywood Reporter has exclusively learned. The annual outdoor hockey game is scheduled for New Year’s Eve in Salt Lake City, Utah. The Utah Mammoth, who joined the league as an expansion team in 2024, will host their first-ever edition of the Winter Classic at Rice Eccles Stadium against the Colorado Avalanche. The Mammoth become the 32nd NHL franchise to participate in the outdoor event — a regular-season game for the teams. Related Stories TV Where to Watch the 2026 NASCAR Cup Series Championship Race Live Online Business Bob Iger's Son to Call Games for Lakers G League Team Boone, fresh off his Wanted Man tour, is set to perform during the first intermission of the game during a performance presented by Ticketmaster, according to a release. The pop star is known for his energetic performances, which often include a flip — or two. The 24-year-old broke out with his chart-topping single “Beautiful Things,” which helped earn him a best new artist nomination at the 2025 Grammy Awards. “The Winter Classic is always about creating something unforgettable, and this year we’re taking that to another level. We’re turning the stadium into a true winter wonderland, and Benson Boone is the perfect artist to bring it to life,” NHL president of events and content Steve Mayer said in a statement. “He’s an incredible performer with a real sense of showmanship, and we can’t wait to see what he does on this stage to create a memorable experience for the fans in the stadium and everyone tuning in from home.” The NHL recently had a slew of musical acts perform during the first intermission of the recent Heritage Classic, which took place at Princess Auto Stadium in Winnipeg, Manitoba, at the end of October. The matchup featured two Canadian teams, the Winnipeg Jets and the Montreal Canadiens. Off Campus star Ella Bright hosted the Heritage Classic intermission show. The musical acts — Remi Wolf, Wolf Parade, Feist and G Flip — were an homage to Heated Rivalry and Off Campus , the two popular hockey romance shows that dominated pop culture over the last year. The Discover NHL Winter Classic will air on TNT, HBO Max and TruTV in the U.S and TVAS in Canada beginning at 4 p.m. Mountain Time. Tickets to the game are available through Ticketmaster . THR

title: Kate Berlant And John Early To Co-Host Film Independent Spirit Awards
full_text: Skip to main content By Patrick Hipes Patrick Hipes Executive Managing Editor More Stories By Patrick Austin Film Festival Reveals Audience Award Winners, Sets Dates For 2027 Film & Script Competitions ‘Elsinore’s Andrew Scott To Receive Palm Springs’ Desert Palm Achievement Award, Actor Palm Springs Film Awards Honorees: ‘La Bola Negra’ To Receive International Star Award View All November 11, 2026 8:38am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kate Berlant and John Early Sela Shiloni Comic duo Kate Berlant and John Early have been set to co-host the 42nd annual Film Independent Spirit Awards , which take place March 6, 2027 at the Hollywood Palladium. It will mark the latest team-up for the pair, which have collaborated on numerous projects including the sketch series 555 and the 2022 comedy special Would It Kill You to Laugh? which scored them an Emmy nomination for writing. Most recently, Berlant appeared in Early’s feature directorial debut Maddie’s Secret , in which he also starred. Related Stories News Roman Coppola Named Creative Consultant For 2027 Spirit Awards Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More “If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” Film Independent president Juan Devis said in a release Wednesday revealing the news. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.” Previous Spirit Awards hosts include SNL alum Ego Nwodim last year, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg and John Waters. Watch on Deadline Nominations for the 2027 Spirit Awards are due December 2 ahead of the ceremony, for which Roman Coppola was recently tapped in a newly created Creative Consultant role. This year’s Spirits will also feature two new categories: Best International First Feature and a Digital Creator Award. title: From a ‘Hell House’ to ‘The Woods,’ Stephen Cognetti Proves His Versatility as a Scary Movie Maestro
full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:30am PT From a ‘Hell House’ to ‘The Woods,’ Stephen Cognetti Proves His Versatility as a Scary Movie Maestro By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest Variety Announces Program for Inaugural Women of Awards Season High Tea 23 hours ago The Team Unveils New Board as Firm Regroups After Rebrand From Wasserman 1 day ago Danielle Fishel Gets Honest About ‘Girl Meets World’ Pay, Says She Knew She Was Disliked on Set for Setting Boundaries (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy photo Stephen Cognetti ’s newest film is a hard pivot from the franchise that made him a household name in horror. Cognetti, who wrote and directed all five chapters in the found footage “ Hell House LLC ” franchise, just finished filming his latest feature, “ A Body in the Woods .” It stars Emma Roberts as Alice Lincoln, a turn-of-the-century woman who lives in a remote cabin in an area of the woods that might be haunted by a witch. Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize Invercine, Gema Films and Gaman Cine, Top Producers on Latin America’s Film-TV Scene, Bring to Market New Productions Manifest Pictures is launching international sales for the film at AFM . Cognetti spoke with Variety about his dark new vision, his influences and the future of “Hell House LLC.” How did you come up with the idea for this new film? I actually wrote this right after the fourth “Hell House” movie. I felt like I was in a very good state of mind, scare-wise. It was the quickest first draft of a script I’ve ever written. I got the idea, and it just flowed. What did Emma’s performance bring to the film? She’s not only a wonderful actress, but she’s just so creatively intelligent. She has all of these good instincts. She just gets things better than anyone I’ve ever worked with on screen. Every discussion with her is on another level because she understood everything. From what we were doing behind the camera to what she was doing on screen, she just has a great understanding. Were there any movies you were inspired by for the look of “A Body in the Woods?” There were two films that really inspired me. The first is not horror at all, but it’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” When I was writing this, I was not only always thinking about the visuals; I was also listening to the soundtrack the entire time. “Assassination” was always in my head. Also, Robert Eggers’ “The Witch” is a film that I just adore. I love everything he did with the camera. It is a very deliberate movement, slow movement, and the camera takes its time. We take our time story-wise; we take our time with the scares, the story. I wouldn’t call this a slow burn at all, but I just love the style of a well-paced, slower horror film, rather than something like I’m used to in the found footage world, which is very jumpy and we’re hopping around quickly, getting to scare after scare. Here we’re just building a world and building a character who’s mostly isolated. How are you a different director from when you first began? You’ve got to learn to pivot quickly. It has gotten a lot easier with every subsequent film, just because I’ve learned how to strategize better and how to put together a game plan for every day. When something’s not working, that experience helps a lot. Will there eventually be another “Hell House LLC” movie? There is a future story. The fifth one, for better or for worse, ended on a cliffhanger, and that was always the intention. But making those films is impossible for where I’m at right now, for a lot of behind-the-scenes reasons. But I would always love to tell more of the story. I just don’t know how it would ever be able to happen. It might come in other forms. I’ve always said that there might be a novel, a graphic novel, to not only tell the final chapter, but also flesh out more of the story that we’ve seen. In terms of a movie, there’s nothing on the horizon yet, but I would never say never. ‘Logan’ Star Dafne Keen Says ‘I Was Offered Cocaine’ as an 11-Year-Old in Hollywood and Hugh Jackman ‘Made Sure No One Abused My Hours’ on Set Loading comments...

title: WME Signs Investigative Journalist Mariana Van Zeller
full_text: Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Paul Wesley Latest To Join Netflix’s ‘Icebreaker’ ‘Chucky’ Creator Don Mancini Signs With Independent Artist Group Lisa Edelstein, Kevin Pollak & Joe Swanberg Among New Additions To SM Goldberger’s ‘Your Heart Is A Hummingbird’ View All November 11, 2026 8:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mariana van Zeller Miguel Angelo EXCLUSIVE: Mariana van Zeller , the Peabody and Emmy Award-winning journalist, filmmaker and co-founder of Muck Media, has signed with WME for representation in all areas. Known for her reporting as a leading authority on the global shadow economy, Van Zeller has led investigations into the opioid crisis, immigration and the explosion of scamming as a global industry. The latter is the subject of her new feature doc Super Scam Me , released Oct. 17 on Hulu, Disney+ and National Geographic. As co-founder of Muck Media, Van Zeller hosted and executive produced their flagship series Trafficked with Mariana van Zeller for National Geographic. The series earned 16 Emmy wins and 88 nominations over five seasons. Other Muck Media titles include the Emmy-nominated Sundance doc Science Fair , Netflix’s Mucho Mucho Amor and The Fall of El Mayo , and HBO Max’s American Pain . Born and raised in Portugal, Van Zeller studied journalism at Columbia University. Her work has been recognized with a Peabody Award, a duPont-Columbia Award, a Television Academy Honor and the Livingston Award for Young Journalists. She also hosts The Hidden Third , a weekly podcast about crime, black markets and the people who live inside them. Watch on Deadline WME will work with Van Zeller to expand her business across documentaries, television, digital audio and video, publishing and beyond. The journalist continues to be managed by Michael Lasker and Nate Dixon at Mosaic. title: Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards
full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:26am PT Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest Kate Berlant and John Early to Host Film Independent Spirit Awards 30 minutes ago Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE) 18 hours ago Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment? 22 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sela Shiloni Kate Berlant and John Early , two of comedy’s most gloriously unpredictable performers, will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards . The 42nd annual celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027, at the Hollywood Palladium, eight days before the 99th Academy Awards on March 14. The date marks a later slot on the calendar and a return to Saturday after this past year’s Sunday, Feb. 15 ceremony, which was hosted by “Saturday Night Live” alum Ego Nwodim. Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize Cineplex Boards Sanfic Title ‘La Residencia’ From ‘Algo Azul' Director Mariel García Spooner “If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” says Film Independent President Juan Devis. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.” The hosts are ready for the assignment. “We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one. Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!” Berlant and Early say in a joint statement. Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg and John Waters. Friends and creative collaborators for more than a decade, Berlant and Early have built a devoted following on a distinctive brand of absurdist comedy that blends sharp social satire, improvisation and performances that rarely go where you expect. Their joint work includes the acclaimed sketch series “555” and the Emmy-nominated Peacock comedy special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” which took familiar comedic conventions and twisted them into something entirely their own. Individually, both have carved out celebrated careers across film, television and live comedy. Berlant’s film credits include “Sorry to Bother You,” “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood” and “Don’t Worry Darling,” and she has appeared in FX’s comedy-drama series “The Bear.” She also earned acclaim for her one-woman show “Kate” and her comedy specials “Cinnamon in the Wind” and “Parmesan.” Early is best known for his breakout performance in the dark comedy series “Search Party,” which ran on TBS before moving to HBO Max, as well as his stand-up special “Now More Than Ever.” He recently made his feature directorial debut with “Maddie’s Secret,” which also features Berlant. This year’s ceremony adds two new categories, best international first feature and the Digital Creator Award, expanding the show’s reach across platforms. Filmmaker Roman Coppola will also bring his artistic vision to the show in the newly created role of creative consultant.The Nominee Brunch, the annual gathering that honors all nominees and features the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, returns to The London West Hollywood on Saturday, Jan. 9, 2027. title: Peacock Phasing In Mobile Updates, With Vertical ‘Voice’ Clips, More Home Screen Sports, Browsing Tweaks & More
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Film Accelerator Open Cities, Run By Ex-Sundance CEO Joana Vicente & Producer Jason Kliot, Reveals First Projects ‘Tangles’ Cast Members Seth Rogen, Julia Louis-Dreyfus & Bryan Cranston On Animated Film’s Rare Back Story AMC Global Media Posts Mixed Q3, Previews ‘The Walking Dead’ AMC+ Bow View All November 11, 2026 8:07am Add us as a Google Preferred Source NBCUniversal ‘s Peacock is ushering in a number of updates to its mobile app, overhauling the browsing experience, putting more sports on the home screen and expanding its vertical video offerings. The updates encompass a wide range of features, from overhauled browsing to a “jump back in” button to an influx of vertical video spanning clips and microdramas. The strategic goal of the updates is to connect with subscribers at key moments throughout the day and increase viewing time, recognizing the role that mobile devices now play in the streaming ecosystem. Just as traditional mobile players like YouTube have been leaning into the living room, legacy media players like NBCU are putting increasing emphasis on their mobile offerings after beginning on their most familiar device, the TV screen. Related Stories News How The 'Married At First Sight UK' Scandal Has Impacted Hit Show Around The World News HBO Max-Paramount+ Bundle Set To Launch In Early 2027, David Ellison Confirms Last month, NBCU parent Comcast said Peacock delivered its second straight quarter of profitability during the third quarter, though its subscriber level stayed flat at 48 million. Watch on Deadline During a press briefing in New York on Tuesday, Matt Strauss, Chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group, said he wasn’t at all discouraged by Peacock’s scale six-plus years after its launch. He pointed to the long-term strategy of the service, which started up at a very different moment for the media business, when ad-free binge releases seemed like the inevitable future. Peacock initially was mostly focused on its free, ad tier, and today still has 80% of its subscribers on its cheaper ad-supported plan. “We arguably didn’t build Peacock to win a streaming war. We built Peacock for growth in the aftermath of a streaming war,” Strauss said. “And that’s where I think we are right now, which is the next phase of growth is going to be around who can win another hour per user per month. And to go and evaluate through that lens, you have to think differently about the user experience. And the phone and mobile has to be a first-class citizen.” Testing is already under way on many of the features, which will go live and be updated continuously through early 2027. Peacock is enhancing its search capabilities with conversational AI, looking to enhance personalization. The updates build on existing features like Your Bravoverse, Clips Feed, and Peacock Performance View. John Jelley, SVP of Product and UX for the NBCUniversal Media Group, emphasized the company’s efforts to tailor its AI approach to the streaming realm. “We combine that in what we call a large action model,” he said during the press briefing. “Rather than predicting the next word as LLMs do, we’re actually predicting the next action.” Vertical video has been on Peacock for nearly two years now, with the service pioneering the format for live sports. NBCU’s long-term rights deal with the NBA, which began in 2025, offered an opportunity to showcase the technology, which will now be expanding to shows like NBC mainstay The Voice . Other sports like college basketball and golf will also get the vertical treatment. Microdramas, which have grown into a multi-billion-dollar category and are seen as a potent on-ramp for streaming viewers, will be an increasing presence on Peacock. At least one new micro title will land on the service each week, the company is promising. These series are generally licensed from third parties but in some cases are commissioned in-house, as in the case of Bravo scripted microdramas like the recently premiered Charmed by a Southern Monster . Spanish-language NBCU subsidiary Telemundo has already been pushing into the microdrama space. “NBCUniversal has an unmatched ability to turn the shows, sports and stories fans love into experiences that extend well beyond the screen,” said Jim Denney, Chief Product Officer, Global Streaming & NBCUniversal Media Group. “Our ambition is for Peacock to be more than a place to watch. With this new mobile experience, we’re evolving Peacock into an entertainment platform that gives fans more ways to discover, participate and strengthen their connection to their favorite stories, teams and franchises, turning viewing into deeper engagement and lasting fandom and loyalty.” Peacock is exploring new setups on its home screen to help viewers quickly “jump back in” to programming they enjoy. Hubs devoted to key franchises will lead not only to episodic fare but also games, microdramas, podcasts, clips and other related material. title: M. John Harrison On Early Adaptation Interest & Why He Almost Added ‘A Film’ To His Booker-Winning Novel’s Title
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart M. John Harrison On Early Adaptation Interest & Why He Almost Added ‘A Film’ To His Booker-Winning Novel’s Title Charlie Sheen’s ‘Mostly Sheenius’ Podcast Lines Up Michael Douglas As First Guest: Rob Lowe, Martin Sheen & Denise Richards Also Set To Appear Web Summit Cancels Day Two As Storm Charles Hits Lisbon View All November 11, 2026 8:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source M. John Harrison Wiktor Szymanowicz/Getty Images With interest in a big-screen adaptation, M. John Harrison has told Deadline he wanted to call his Booker Prize -winning novel ‘ The End of Everything : A Film’, but got cold feet at the last minute. Harrison won the Booker for ‘The End of Everything’, to give his book its final title. It follows a beachcomber living on the English coast after a disaster has struck. He finds a mysterious object in the sea and brings it inland. As well as spurring book sales, there is always sharp interest in adapting Booker titles. ‘The End of Everything’ has distinctive landscapes and characters as well as mysterious shape-shifting alien entities called the iGhetti. Related Stories News M. John Harrison Wins The 2026 Booker Prize With 'The End Of Everything' News Douglas Stuart, Marlon James & Elizabeth Strout Among 13 Authors On The Booker Prize Longlist; Organizers Say 2026 Selection "Rewards Risk" Fresh from winning the prestigious literary award, Harrison told Deadline that he visualized scenes from the book as he wrote them, and noted, as have others, that his novel has a cinematic quality. Watch on Deadline “When I’ve constructed a scene, when I turn it into words, I can see it. And I was, in fact, going to subtitle this novel ‘The End of Everything: A Film’. I lost my nerve at the last minute, but I now really wish I’d done it, because it’s got the structure of a kind of middle-European film, with the right provenance to be very watchable indeed.” The book is published by the Serpent’s Tail imprint, marking its first Booker win. Similarly, it was the first win for 81-year-old Harrison who served as a Booker judge in 2022. “We do have some interest, it hasn’t gone far enough to be able to talk about [in detail], but there is interest in doing something,” the writer told Deadline when asked if an adaptation was in the works. Harrison would rather his book came to screen as a movie than a series. His take is it would be a European-flavored film, with someone of the ilk of late and pioneering Hungarian director Béla Tarr at the helm. “I think for me, personally, if it were to happen, that it would be a film. And it would remind you either of a difficult French film, or a Béla Tarr film,” Harrison said. The author is an avowed movie fan, but whether he would be involved in any adaptation of his lauded book is not clear. “I watch lots of films, I love films,” he said. “But it’s like art, I see a lot of paintings, but I don’t know a great deal about how they’re painted and therefore I wouldn’t feel entirely comfortable being involved in a process like that.” He added that he could envisage how the book might work on screen, and how an adaptation could win his approval. “There are ways that that that book would have to be done to be made into a film that made me excited – that continued my excitement from writing the book – but I have faith that I might find somebody who could do that.” Booker Chief Executive Gaby Wood has also noted the filmic qualities in ‘The End of Everything’ and has said: “Readers will also recognize many tropes from cinema: the disaster movie, the road movie, the couple on the run, the noir heroine with a gun in her bag, the apocalypse.” Harrison pushes against classifications such as science fiction although that is the genre his work, stretching to 13 novels, is placed in. full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Days Of Our Lives’ Actor James Reynolds Reveals Parkinson’s Diagnosis; Condition Being Written Into Storyline ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ With Tom Hiddleston & Hayley Atwell Sells Out, Tops $2M Gross; ‘Here There Are Blueberries’, ‘Downstate’, ‘Fantasticks’ Fill Seats – Broadway Box Office Richard Schiff Among Cast Added To Broadway’s ‘Awake And Sing!’ Revival View All November 11, 2026 8:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source James Reynolds at 2018 Daytime Emmy Awards Getty James Reynolds , who has played Abe Carver on Days of Our Lives for 45 years, has revealed that he’s been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and that his condition will be worked into the storyline of the long-running soap. In an interview with ET (watch it below), Reynolds, 80, concedes that he initially tried to mask his symptoms while on set but that he was increasingly unsuccessful. Asked about the decision to address the diagnosis within the storyline, Reynolds said, “Well, it kind of goes back to when I thought I was hiding it. The writers also wanted to incorporate because it was obvious. It was obvious. And we play life here.” Related Stories News 'Days Of Our Lives' Actor Robert Kelker-Kelly's Cause Of Death Revealed Casting 'Days Of Our Lives' Casts Long-Awaited Dominic Marino Reynolds continued, “And there are many other characters who have gone through real-life issues that then are mirrored on the show, and this is an issue that it is going to be mirrored on the show and there’s nothing any of us can really do about it.” Watch on Deadline The actor, who is the longest-running Black actor in a single series in television history, said he feels his character is particularly well-suited to the storyline. “I feel like the value of Abe as a character [is he] overcomes a lot, has tremendous amount of strength, deals with a lot of things with humor as well as understanding.” Reynolds, who has kept his diagnosis private except for family for a few years, says the symptoms – shaky hands, occasional balance issues, sometimes a shortness of breath – become increasingly difficult to conceal. “I thought I was hiding it but I wasn’t. You play that game with yourself.” The actor said in the last few weeks he realized he might have been showing early symptoms – “horrible dreams” that caused him to thrash and fall out of bed – as long as 15 to 20 years ago, a realization he said he came to after watching actor Alan Alda’s recent interview on C BS Sunday Morning, during which Alda said his earliest Parkinsons symptom was acting out his dreams. title: Peacock Overhauls Mobile App for Vertical Video Era in Effort to “Win Another Hour Per User, Per Month”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peacock Peacock mobile users might want to check their app store for updates — the NBCUniversal streaming platform is undergoing its largest mobile revamp ever. Peacock mobile 2.0 (it’s probably well beyond 2.0, but stick with us here) is designed to, in part, “win another hour per user, per month,” Matt Strauss , chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group, told a small group of reporters including The Hollywood Reporter on Tuesday. Peacock has been profitable for two straight quarters now, and it’s part of Strauss’s job to keep it that way. To accomplish that reasonable-sounding goal, NBCU is overhauling Peacock’s smartphone display and functionality for the vertical video craze, which it boasts as having been early money on, as well as the Comcast entertainment brand’s fandoms and its sports content. Peacock users who use the app on both their TV and smartphone double the engagement of those who only sign in on their television. As John Jelley, the group’s senior vice president of product and UX (user experience), sees it, today’s opportunity is on the smaller of the two screens. “Every streamer today is really a sea of sameness on the homepage. Because they’ve taken a TV experience and largely ported it over, they are expecting the user to do the sorting,” Jelley said. “We see an opportunity to recognize what a fan is trying to accomplish in that session and make the next most useful action easier to find.” “We recognize that we have to start thinking of ourselves less as a streaming platform and more of an entertainment platform,” Strauss said. “How do we super serve our franchises and our fandoms where the best experience is on our app?” To those ends, “conversational AI search” will help users find what they want even if they don’t know how to directly express it. Short clips that lead to full episodes will expedite and elongate engagement, and franchise/fandom hubs can be a one-stop shop for fans of the Bravo-verse, for one standout example. There will also be games (like Law & Order: Clue Hunter and Public Eye ) and a membership program “giving eligible subscribers exclusive rewards, benefits and activities tied to the movies and shows they enjoy,” per the official announcement. One particularly cool idea is adaptive live viewing. Peacock plans to expand its live vertical video tests to The Voice live simulcasts, NCAA basketball games and, in a clear direct response to the rise of YouTube Golf, you guessed it: golf. A “dynamic video player” will switch between vertical and horizontal video playback automatically depending on the device orientation, keeping key action in frame. NBA games will soon get the same treatment, with “easy access to player stats” and “deeper game information sitting directly underneath the live feed in a dual screen view,” the executives say. Finally, these days, you cannot talk about vertical video without discussing microdramas . Jelley discusses them frankly, because he says that’s how his users speak about them. “When we talk to users about microdramas, they’re not embarrassed by them. They don’t feel that they’re something they’ll just do in private,” Jelley said. “They’re watching them at home at different moments of the day, they’re watching them on the commute. We are very committed to premium long-form content, and that has a massive place not only on the phone, but also on TV. But this is really another modality.” THR

title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy Elevate Peacock’s Overly Familiar Southern-Fried Thriller
full_text: × Skip to main content By Daniel Fienberg Plus Icon Daniel Fienberg Chief Television Critic TheFienPrint Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Meghann Fahy (left) and Rose Byrne in ‘The Good Daughter.' Mark Hill/PEACOCK Logo text We all have our television pet peeves and, for me, red flags abound in Peacock ‘s new limited series, The Good Daughter . Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her book of the same name, The Good Daughter is interchangeable, in terms of title, plot or structure, with a dozen recent limited series — most conspicuously, Amazon’s The Better Sister and Netflix’s His & Hers . The Good Daughter The Bottom Line A strong cast makes up for familiar irritations. Airdate: Thursday, November 12 (Peacock) Cast: Rose Byrne, Meghann Fahy, Brendan Gleeson, Olivia Williams, Harper Steele, Michael Dorman, Audrey Grace Marshall, Drew Cheek Creator: Karin Slaughter Director: Steph Green It’s a story set in and filmed in the Deep South, but its central cast is populated by actors from Australia, Ireland, Massachusetts and basically anywhere other than the Deep South, leading to a succotash of colorful and, to put it politely, inconsistent accents. Related Stories TV 'O.J.'s Accomplice' Has Its Own 'The Jinx' Hot Mic Moment TV Matthew Weiner Out as Showrunner of Eddie Murphy Peacock Series After Clash With Producers And it’s a story instigated by a school shooting and pushed forward by multiple instances of sexual violence, all propping up a mystery that’s barely mysterious — at least until the characters all sit down to explain everything in a series of weakly staged monologues. That The Good Daughter is so full of tropes I find tedious or annoying and yet somehow ends up being compulsively entertaining is a tribute to Slaughter’s gift for characterization and dialogue, the confident hand of series director Steph Green, and particularly the committed, emotionally exposed and often funny performances from leads Meghann Fahy , Rose Byrne and Brendan Gleeson . The Good Daughter begins with a double dose of trauma, the better to winnow away squeamish viewers. First, in flashback, devoted sisters Sam (Audrey Grace Marshall) and Charlie (Drew Cheek) witness a horrible act of violence perpetrated on their doting mother (Olivia Williams’ Gamma), perhaps the latest retaliation against their father (Gleeson’s Rusty), a defense attorney prone to rubbing people the wrong way. Their lives will never be the same. Jump to the present. Charlie (Fahy) has grown up to follow in her father’s footsteps, working out of his ramshackle office in the same Georgia town populated by people who still hate him and don’t feel too kindly toward her. She’s separated from hubby Ben (Michael Dorman, endearingly normal in a show populated by broad portrayals) and making various self-destructive choices, including a one-night stand with Huck (Jake McDorman), whose ponytail and scruff let you know he’s a bad idea. Charlie and Huck accidentally swap phones, which leads her to discover that he’s a high school teacher. In the process of returning his phone, she is present when Kelly (Shayna Benardo, an impressively grounding force) shows up and shoots and kills the well-liked principal and a freshman. Rusty, who has a bad cough and a history of heart problems, and likes to wear — for reasons that are never explained — a red clown nose, shows up to represent Kelly, whose cognitive issues haven’t stopped the local powerbrokers from eyeing the death penalty. Sensing everything is going astray, Rusty also calls elder daughter Sam (Byrne), now a patent lawyer in New York City and left with a permanent limp and partial blindness stemming from the incident with her mother. Sam hasn’t seen or talked to Charlie in 10 years, but she quickly finds herself back in Pikeville, caught up in the mystery of the shooting, as well as several additional mysteries from her family’s past. If you just look at the bones of the series, The Good Daughter is beyond rudimentary, with a crime in the present and a crime in the past that just coincidentally happen to be directly connected. The story can barely even decide what twists are supposed to be surprising and, as a result, nothing is really “guessable” or revelatory. Instead, The Good Daughter works best as a dirtied-up — though confusingly racially whitewashed — version of To Kill a Mockingbird , with Rusty as a lawyer doing noble things in a disreputable way, constantly looking like he slept at his desk, bottle in hand, eschewing Atticus Finch’s seersucker and moral rectitude. He stands up to threats from his adversaries that are violent and gory rather than ominous and insinuated, investigating cases in which the rape and persecution of the handicapped and impoverished play out on the surface rather than being buried in euphemism. It almost certainly works better on the page than on the screen, where we’ve seen too many versions of these generic rednecks in their generic pick-ups and these generic drawling, obfuscating lawmen to take them seriously. Green and the series’ cinematographers are able to embed in the rundown streets of Pikeville and take us into the “holler,” capturing this community within a community. But when every main cast member talks like the closest they’ve ever been to a holler was a quick drive-through during rehearsal, the verisimilitude suffers. What holds the show together is Slaughter’s grasp on the characters and their relationships. When Sam, Charlie and Rusty talk, it’s in a vernacular that mixes in-jokes, deeply felt family history, snooty literary references (lots of Flannery O’Connor and Emily Dickinson), amusingly unsnooty pop culture references (from Die Hard to Buffy the Vampire Slayer ), and an awareness of how to hurt or heal the people they know best. Byrne, Fahy and Gleeson don’t talk like they come from the same place, but the energy among them gives the series its energy and its authenticity. Sure, Fahy is doing a variation on her bad sister character from Netflix’s Sirens , but she’s tremendous at playing these open books of damage. A little too much of Byrne’s performance consists of actorly takes on disability, but she makes those notes of artificiality pay off. Everything Sam does is a put-on; her attire, hair and speech are defined in opposition to the place she left behind and hoped never to return to, with aspects of her natural self returning as she spends more time in Pikeville. It’s easy to buy them as sisters, in both the parts evoking pain and the parts where they bicker humorously. Plus, it’s easy to see the toll taken by trauma and time because Byrne and Fahy are well-matched by Marshall and Cheek. Gleeson isn’t as convincing in the flashback segments, and his Southern-ish intonations kept reminding me of somebody I couldn’t quite place, but he makes Rusty rascally and flawed. Like the actors, the characters are occupying roles — the city mouse, the bad girl, the folksy country lawyer — but when they’re together, they can be themselves. It’s a nice touch that one of the few characters who doesn’t have a public role to play, Rusty’s longtime assistant Lenore, is played by Harper Steele — you know her from the documentary Will & Harper — who isn’t an actor and comes across not as studied but as gentle and natural. For five episodes, Green maintains the flow between past and present smoothly, and is able to modulate most of the agonizing parts of the story so that they feel tense but not exploitative. Too bad the finale collapses under the weight of all its over-explaining. I never quite cared who did what and why, but Fahy, Byrne and Gleeson at least made it possible to care about the people to whom these things were happening. THR

title: AI Audio Startup ElevenLabs Expands Nvidia Collaboration Amid CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair Scandal
full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:00am PT AI Audio Startup ElevenLabs Expands Nvidia Collaboration Amid CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair Scandal By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Nvidia Stock and AI World Rocked by CEO Jensen Huang’s Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy 22 hours ago AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion 1 day ago Elvis Music Owners, Eminem Publisher File Sprawling New Lawsuits Against AI Music Generator Suno: ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick Up a Guitar’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images ElevenLabs is keeping its yearslong Nvidia partnership strong, no matter the national-security chaos enveloping the chipmaker’s CEO . The AI audio startup said on Wednesday during its New York Summit it would expand its partnership with Nvidia to power its suite of voice agents, dubbed ElevenAgents, with the tech provider’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, its latest open model that helps power AI agents’ understanding of workflows and human reasoning. Nvidia last year became an ElevenLabs investor, complete with a splashy produced video posted to Staniszewski’s LinkedIn page. title: Skydance Succession: As David Ellison Sets His Team, Heads Are Rolling as Hollywood Finds Out Who’s Really in Charge
full_text: Illustration by Will Hooks Of all the things keeping David Ellison up at night, the countdown to 2028 may be the most pressing. At least that’s what many media observers and Hollywood insiders believe. Ellison’s anxiety, they say, isn’t fueled by the forthcoming presidential election or the Olympic Games that will descend on Los Angeles, where Ellison now owns two iconic studio lots. Instead, his agita is arising from the 8 movies he still needs to acquire or produce in 2028 to reach the magic number of 30 — that’s the benchmark Skydance pledged to meet annually in order to close the $111 billion acquisition that made his company a content behemoth. Related Stories Sanfic Mórbido Lab Lineup Ranges From an LGBTQ Alien Monster Comedy to a Mapuche Parable, Extreme Horror and Cold War Sci-Fi ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America Between Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures, 22 films have been dated for 2028 so far. A large number of those — like “Gremlins 3,” Baz Luhrmann’s rumored Joan of Arc biopic and an untitled movie from the Duffer brothers — have yet to start production. And, of course, Hollywood is keeping a close watch on how the new regime handles the urgent task of closing deals with Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig for a “ Barbie ” follow-up. Zohar Lazar Despite Skydance’s other pledge — to streamline costs via cutting-edge technology — feature films remain one of the most expensive gambles in the business (and that’s if audiences respond). The challenge before Ellison and his team is to churn out hits fast — not just to prove their hotly debated merger will be viable in the long run but to generate the cash needed to pay down the combined company’s staggering $80 billion debt. Five weeks in, if Team Ellison is losing sleep about the operational challenges ahead, it’s not letting that on to the media. “People are viewing our $30 billion-plus content spend as an expense, but content is our asset,” Skydance chief financial officer Dennis Cinelli told Variety , speaking ahead of the company’s third-quarter earnings report. “Whether it’s for our theatrical or TV business, both of our streaming platforms, third-party sales, the networks portfolio — we’re investing in content because it has proved tremendously valuable. We’re confident we can drive growth and increase profitability and cash flow.” On Nov. 9, as Skydance unveiled its first quarterly earnings report as a combined company, leadership said a big push will come in early 2027 to offer consumers a bundle of the streaming services now under the Skydance roof: HBO Max and Paramount+. The price will come at a competitive discount designed to allow Skydance to gain market share among subscribers, one source says. Skydance plans to offer a fully integrated service that puts both brands on a single platform — which will make it easier for the company to keep viewers moving around its streaming universe — by 2029. There is much speculation that the company will eventually retire the Paramount+ moniker, given that HBO is the more powerful consumer brand. Meanwhile, Skydance is touting the power of its portfolio: A combined 205-million streaming subscribers in more than 100 global territories, a library of roughly 15,000 films and more than 100,000 hours of TV series. Hollywood’s new colossus has a content library larger than its studio rivals’ by a significant factor, even if its stewards change, as James Gunn and Peter Safran found out the hard way this week. (The DC Studios chiefs made it just five weeks into the Skydance regime before Ellison announced on earnings day that he would replace the pair with producer Jeremy Latcham, an early architect of Marvel Studios.) Superman, Batman and many other characters in the Skydance vault represent a treasure trove of the kind of IP that can yield new adaptations and spinoffs for decades. The chance to buy Warner Bros.’ vault was so attractive that last year even Netflix, the leader in global streaming, was driven to give up its build-not-buy philosophy regarding big acquisitions to chase Warner Bros. and HBO — until Ellison stuck his foot in the door and refused to leave without a deal. Streaming is the engine of the future for Skydance. But in the short term, the company’s fate will be determined by that of its linear cable channels. With the merger, Skydance hasn’t just doubled down on this sector — it has tripled down; Skydance has by far the industry’s collection of linear cable channels. Its TV portfolio is anchored by CBS and spans some 55 cable networks, including CNN, TNT, TBS, Cartoon Network, TCM, Nickelodeon, Comedy Central, BET, Discovery, TLC, Food Network and HGTV. But the traditional business of cable television is deteriorating; subscribers are slowly but surely giving up on linear cable services in favor of streaming platforms. The erosion of once-reliable cable TV profits has bedeviled Hollywood’s majors for more than a decade and has been a catalyst for the latest round of merger mania. As was the case for Paramount and WBD when they were separate companies, the enlarged Skydance remains heavily dependent on linear TV for cash flow and profits — and the cable and satellite biz remains a steadily melting iceberg. In the second quarter of this year, for example, Paramount’s TV business revenue slid 9% to $3.1 billion, but the segment still delivered all of the company’s adjusted $1.1 billion earnings for the quarter. Skydance’s ability to meet its post-merger financial targets hinges on whether the TV business crumbles faster than Ellison and his financial engineers have projected, and whether streaming sees commensurate growth to make up for it. That’s a lot to leave to fate. Here’s the quandary: Skydance must slash costs while investing in content and paying down its immense $80 billion in net debt. The numbers may not add up. “[W]e are concerned more aggressive cost-cutting measures in TV media could leave the segment vulnerable to a faster-than-expected rate of revenue declines,” MoffettNathanson analyst Robert Fishman wrote in an Oct. 23 research note. Industry veterans have watched the creation of Skydance with wonderment. More so than Disney’s acquisition of 21st Century Fox, the union of Paramount and Warner Bros. feels like a milestone transition for the motion picture business that emerged in the 1910s and ’20s around silent films. Both iconic studios were foundational brand names for entertainment back then, and there is great hope among the many industry insiders who have worked across both that those proud logos and studio lots will endure for another century. After finally closing the WBD acquisition, Skydance leadership opened themselves up to a media firing squad on the Paramount lot in early October. Ellison and team addressed burning questions about real estate, cash flow, layoffs and more. Yet inside the company, rank-and-file employees across both operations feel left in the dark. Conversations with staffers in many corners of the Skydance business yielded a feeling of “radio silence,” as one person put it, from the top as pink slips loom and anxiety around greenlights and general spending persists. On balance, another source inside the company deadpanned: “It’s been about a month” since the two entertainment giants combined (Skydance had no comment on the matter). Skydance’s CEO David Ellison, left, and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, right, pose for a picture on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 8. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura Who can blame them, as the town places bets on whether Ellison will have the cash to pay back his lenders. Skydance’s interest expenses are expected to be more than $6 billion next year. According to financial projections, the company intends to reduce that debt load from a figure that is seven times larger than its adjusted annual earnings to a number that is three times larger than adjusted net earnings, which is a more typical debt ratio for large companies. If that model doesn’t hold, Ellison will need to find additional sources of capital. Will his father, billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, whose Ellison Family trust committed $14 billion in equity financing for the WBD takeover, be willing to pump even more money into his son’s gambit to create one of Hollywood’s biggest conglomerates? That remains to be seen. There have also been rumors that David is hunting for more big-money backers to keep Skydance afloat — including Elon Musk. Cinelli told Variety that Skydance is not seeking any additional capital at this time. (Skydance and Musk declined to comment on the tech mogul’s possible involvement.) Skydance’s pledged $30 billion annual spend on new content towers over those of rivals Netflix ($20 billion annually) and Disney ($24 billion in 2026), but investment and prayer alone will not make a meaningful dent in the company’s tremendous liabilities. To that end, bloodletting will come in the form of layoffs (expected by the end of the year and extending into the first quarter of 2027) and ruthless efficiency targets. Insiders at Skydance say cost savings from the company’s acquisition of Paramount Global will blow past an anticipated $2 billion in cuts and approach $3 billion. That’s after only a year in control of the former Shari Redstone empire. Fat-trimming opportunities from the inherited Warner Bros. Discovery books also abound, three sources say. A recent team meeting on the Warner Bros. lot revealed that Skydance will be looking closely at its financial commitments to sporting events like the Olympics. Unexpected (and eyebrow-raising) expenses have been discovered, like trifling luxury costs that amount to “tens of millions” of dollars, per two sources, on hospitality hospitality splurges like dining, travel and gifts. The former WBD regime spent in ways big and small — like stacks of receipts for sandwiches and green juices from the gourmet grocery store Erewhon. There will also be “millions” saved by combining or reducing spends on outside vendors, studio services, redundant marketing budgets and more (one source even suggests press junkets will be revamped. Sorry, journalists: No more sushi at the Four Seasons. And Ellison’s executive table prides itself on its strong, effective characters. Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, a respected operator and the former CEO of Mattel, has claimed daily operations as his purview. President Andy Gordon and CFO Cinelli will mind people and the purse, respectively. HBO golden child Casey Bloys sits atop the entire streaming operation with JB Perrette. Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are now at the molten core of the movie business, controlling both Paramount, WB and DC Studios. Former CBS chief George Cheeks now runs all of linear TV and news. And what about David? “There’s a lot of talk about David Ellison. Not since Walt Disney have you had an owner-operator running a major Hollywood company,” says Cinelli. “David is uniquely well-positioned to lead. He’s someone who loves the creative aspect of the business, and wants to spend his time making films and shows with passion. But he also grew up in Silicon Valley. His mentors and most valuable lessons come from that place, and that’s exactly what Skydance needs to succeed in the future.” As any Hollywood executive knows, all the strength in the world cannot account for the exercise in pain that is managing creative budgets. Take the juicy fallout around “Barbie 2” as a case study. As Ellison toiled for almost a year to win WBD, that company was stuck in tense negotiations for a sequel to Warner Bros.’ highest-grossing movie ever: “Barbie.” Director Gerwig and co-screenwriter Noah Baumbach dangled a concept for a sequel in front of now-axed WB film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy. They would not, however, allow a new movie into development until new deals were struck for themselves, producer-star Robbie and her A-list Ken doll Ryan Gosling that reflected the runaway success of the first film. So the negotiations, led by the creative team’s all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd, broke down. The creatives were demanding equal pay, which one person familiar with the deal pegs at around $25 million each for Gerwig, Robbie and Gosling (Baumbach would share in the writing fee with Gerwig, and he conveniently received a new overall deal at Warners while the “Barbie” negotiations were churning). Team “Barbie” also requested increased pieces of the back end, at which point then-WBD CEO David Zaslav balked — shutting down the talks as the studio’s licensing rights to the famous toy faced a year-end deadline for renewal. Ellison, Keisz and Lourd are keen to make the “Barbie 2” deal happen by the end of the year, two sources say, and Kreiz is obviously close to the property as Mattel’s former chief executive. But for a company with an $80 billion debt tab, how does a decreased profit margin make sense? In the view of former Warner Bros. CEO Barry Meyer, the key thing that the new owners need to remember is to invest in creativity. At the end of the day, it’s all about the movies and shows. “Creating value with the content is very, very important. Distribution is usually a lot more commoditized than content,” says Meyer, who spent 41 years at Warner Bros., capped by a 14-year run as CEO. “Content is creative. Content is unique. Streaming is how you get it there, but the content is where the value is.” Todd Spangler and Jennifer Maas contributed to this report. title: Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Nov 11, 2026 8:00am PT Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Daniel Dae Kim and 3AD Board North Korean Defector Documentary ‘School for Defectors’ (EXCLUSIVE) 34 minutes ago ‘Train to Busan’ Director Yeon Sang-ho on AI Thriller ‘Paradise Lost’: ‘Something as Mysterious and Unknowable to Us as a Black Hole’ 55 minutes ago ‘Adolescence’ Writer Jack Thorne Adapts Matt Haig’s ‘The Humans’ for London’s West End With ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Matt Smith 7 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Damien Fry/Changho Lim “Lost” and “Hawaii Five-0” star Daniel Dae Kim and his production company 3AD have joined filmmaker Jeremy Workman’s documentary “ School for Defectors ” as executive producers. The film follows a small South Korean school where every student escaped from North Korea. The film is set at Jangdaehyun School, in an industrial part of Busan. The school has just 20 students, and each of them is a defector from the North. Workman was let into a community that had never been filmed before. His film looks at the young people there in terms of both what they have lived through and the lives ahead of them. Related Stories ‘The Cry of Serankwa,’ an Indigenous Eco-Thriller and Triple Sanfic Industria Award Winner, Strikes Distribution Deal for Latin America Cineplex Boards Sanfic Title ‘La Residencia’ From ‘Algo Azul' Director Mariel García Spooner 3AD joins a producing team that also includes Bearing North , WildBrush Media, SonaFilms and Hooligan Films. “3AD and I are really excited to join ‘School for Defectors’ as executive producers. We believe deeply in the power of documentary filmmaking, and in telling the story of this special high school, Jeremy has poignantly revealed a story full of heart, humor and humanity,” Kim said. “School for Defectors” premiered at the True/False Film Festival in March. Since then it has screened at a dozen more festivals, including Florida, RiverRun, DC/DOX, Calgary, Hamptons, Woodstock, Heartland and Vancouver. It has won six awards so far and is set to screen at Doc NYC. “What we think makes ‘School for Defectors’ so special is that it’s not simply a story about North Korea. It’s a story about youth, hope, and the universal desire to belong,” Workman said. “Daniel Dae Kim has built a remarkable career championing stories and communities that deserve greater visibility, and we’re incredibly honored to have him and 3AD help bring this film to an even wider audience.” Workman, who is repped by UTA, makes portraits of unusual and often obsessive people. His credits include “Secret Mall Apartment” (Netflix), “Lily Topples the World” (Max), “Deciding Vote” (The New Yorker), “The World Before Your Feet” (Prime Video) and “Magical Universe” (AMC+). Across close to 200 reviews, his documentaries hold a combined 95% score on Rotten Tomatoes. Kim earned a Tony nomination for his role in “Yellow Face.” He hosts and executive produces “K-Everything,” a four-part CNN travel series about South Korea’s cultural reach around the world, which premiered May 9. In June, he appeared in Season 2 of “Avatar: The Last Airbender.” Off screen, his testimony before Congress helped get the COVID-19 Hate Crimes Act passed. He has worked with a number of AAPI community groups and served as advisory council co-chair of TAAF. He is repped by CAA, Linden, Gang, Tyre, Ramer, Brown & Passman, and Narrative. Kim set up 3AD in 2014 to make work in every medium and genre built around people who have historically been underrepresented on screen. The company’s credits include ABC hit “The Good Doctor,” Amazon Prime thriller “Butterfly” and IFC documentary “Bad Axe,” which made the Oscar shortlist in 2022. Producer John Cheng runs development at 3AD, which is under a first-look TV pact with 20th Century Studios. title: Entertainment 360 Buys Influencer Firm Brigade As It Expands In Creator Economy

Roger Kisby/Getty Images Entertainment 360 has accelerated its drive into the creator economy by acquiring Brigade, the creative management firm focused on digital talent. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the acquisition brings elite digital tastemakers, including Substack writers, podcasters and influencers, to the Los Angeles-based talent management company run by a collective of partners as it moves beyond traditional film and TV representation. Brigade founder Max Stein will become a partner at Entertainment 360 and bring his team and clients with him to help the combined company tap a growing influencer universe and manage and monetize celebrity creators coveted by brand marketers. “The ways audiences discover and engage with entertainment have changed, and so have the needs of the talent building careers today,” the Entertainment 360 partners said in a statement. “Max recognized this evolution early and he and his exceptional team have built a remarkable business representing exactly the kind of original, forward-thinking talent we have always sought to work with.
