title: Next Gen 2026: 35 Rising Hollywood Executives Under 35
full_text: × Skip to main content The Next Gen execs were photographed Oct. 26 and Oct. 30 at PMC Studios in Los Angeles. Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Nobody ever said that Hollywood careers come easy. But right now, with consolidation and layoffs decimating the middle rungs of entertainment’s steep corporate ladder and studio remits changing with each earnings report, dream jobs have never been more difficult to land, much less retain. Such trends aren’t slowing the ascent of THR ’s Next Gen class of 2026, who join such illustrious alumni as Donna Langley, Ari Emanuel, Kevin Feige and Peter Rice. In fact, this group is too busy forging new paths through the chaos — whether that’s bringing Gen Z back to cinemas (as indie producer Christian Vazquez did with both Primetime and You Can See Everything ) or fortifying the streaming ecosystem amid endless churn (see Claudia Shin and Louie Hayes, behind the Apple TV Emmy darling Widow’s Bay and the Prime Video breakout Sterling Point , respectively.) Meet the 35 executives and reps, each of them 35 years old or younger, who should be atop your call list, if they aren’t already. Alyssa Altman, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion RK Films, senior vp LOGLINE Championing rom-coms like Anyone But You and Netflix’s upcoming 13 Going on 30 update. THE ARC Altman got a unique view of the industry when she would join her father, Steve, who rented out lighting, camera and grip equipment: “I grew up doing my homework in grip trucks, and I just loved being on set.” Her dad’s rom-com adoration rubbed off during their weekly trips to the movies, where films like Love Actually made an early impression. Altman studied journalism at Emerson but caught the producing bug while moonlighting on college TV projects. After time at Gersh, she became then-Universal exec Jeff Kirschenbaum’s assistant and followed him to RK Films. While the company focused on bigger IP plays, she endorsed the script for Anyone But You (“That was my baby”), Sony’s Sydney Sweeney-Glen Powell feature that became a rare theatrical comedy hit. Up next: Amazon MGM’s tennis rom-com Love Love and Netflix’s Millie Bobby Brown-led Just Picture It . PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Andy Cohen. My favorite way to de-stress after a long day is to watch and listen to the soothing sound of people fighting on Bravo.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “The fact that movies geared towards women do great theatrically. Every time it happens, people act like it’s an anomaly. Women are starved for content and it’s not a coincidence.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “When I was an assistant at Universal, we set up a screening for an A-list star who specifically requested popcorn from the Universal Studios theme park. I had to sneak into the park through the back lot and bring it back before he arrived.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Sally Albright from When Harry Met Sally . She isn’t afraid to speak her mind, is a hopeless romantic, and has strong opinions on how she orders her food.” Jenna Berger, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Marvel Studios, director of production development LOGLINE Berger is serving as co-producer, and Kevin Feige’s right hand, on Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars . ’Nuff said. THE ARC An L.A. native with industry parents, Berger grew up wanting to make movies. “I had this theory that everybody who didn’t want to make movies was lying to themselves and secretly did,” she says. So, shortly after graduating from University of Pennsylvania with a double major in English and film, she landed a gig at The Mark Gordon Co. Still, it was Marvel that was making some of her favorite films — she saw Spider-Man: Homecoming four times in the theater — but the company felt impenetrable … until it wasn’t. In 2019, Berger scored a position, rising to junior exec before finding herself the solo exec on the Marvel TV series Ms. Marvel , where she earned a supervising producer credit and honed her creative leadership, talent development and production expertise. “It was the best crash course in figuring out how this company worked and making something worthy of the Marvel name,” she says. The higher-ups took note, which is why Berger now oversees some of the studio’s most ambitious films. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Kermit the Frog. Because my job is to bring amazingly talented people together to make something special amid total chaos … which sometimes means convincing everyone the show must go on before the set falls down around us.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “David Heyman. To get to work on Bond and Harry Potter?! A dream. Would love to trade places for a day … or forever.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Having a sneeze attack while leaving a voicemail for Aaron Sorkin on behalf of my boss.” Natalie Berkus, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion LuckyChap, senior vp TV LOGLINE Developing (and producing) your future TV obsessions, including Andrew Garfield’s Wild Things . THE ARC Rather than follow her agent dad and comedy writer mom into the business, Berkus arrived at University of Michigan eager to be a lawyer. “Then I rushed the law fraternity and didn’t get in,” she says. “I mean, I whiffed it and was like, ‘Shit, now what do I do?’ ” The answer, it turns out, was to parlay her love of TV into a series of PA gigs on shows like The Mindy Project before talking her way into a job as the writers assistant on Girls and, later, with Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s company. From there, she logged six years at Imagine Entertainment, where she was intimately involved in a slate that included The ’Burbs and the upcoming Siegfried and Roy series starring Garfield and Jude Law for Apple TV. But LuckyChap came calling a year ago, and the L.A. native and new mom to daughter Roonie jumped at the opportunity to work at the Margot Robbie-led hit factory. In that time, she has built a roster of 10 to 15 projects, including a Life Is Strange series for Amazon Prime Video. Still, Berkus doesn’t take herself too seriously. “If I had to brand myself, I’d say I like to bring a levity to this business,” she says, “because I think sometimes, especially now, things can get really stressful and we lose sight of the fact that ultimately this is just one big party.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Nina Rosenstein, who does all of the HBO comedy specials. We’ve never met, but Nina, girl, if you’re reading this, let’s link and get our Freaky Friday moment started!” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “That having unapproachable girlboss ‘I’m smarter than you’ energy is cool. It’s not, it’s lame! Normalize the quiet power in validating others and having a fun vibe.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “Nowhere are you crazy!! No more of these!!” Mandi Brooksbank, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Netflix, senior manager, business affairs, scripted series LOGLINE Helps mold Netflix’s scripted slate, brokering deals with top talent like Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media. THE ARC As a kid in Reno, Nevada, Brooksbank figured she was destined for Broadway. While most her age were on the playground, she was busy with casino shows, doing dinner theater (and playing the harp) in vintage Hollywood glam. “It was entertainment or bust,” she recalls with a laugh. Later, she’d speedrun undergrad at USC and law school at Southwestern, finishing both in five years. Since then, she’s built a Hollywood résumé that includes stints at CAA, Donaldson Callif Perez and eOne. Now in her fifth year at Netflix, Brooksbank helps steer the streamer’s scripted series unit, striking deal after deal with TV’s biggest names. It’s a high volume affair, with Brooksbank managing a slate that includes The Altruists , Ransom Canyon and Sirens , among many others. “I’m the third child in a family of six,” she says of her negotiating chops. “They all have big personalities, so they prepared me well for Hollywood.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Miss Piggy.” WHY ISN’T HOLLYWOOD TALKING ABOUT … “Women directors’ second and third films. We talk about breaking through, but what about career longevity?” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “When I was considering law school, Patti Felker encouraged me to see being a woman as an advantage in negotiations, particularly the ability to read people, adapt and adjust your approach to the person across the table without losing sight of what you’re there to accomplish.” Barry Buren, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion CAA, TV talent agent LOGLINE Makes deals for A-listers including Pedro Pascal, Matthew Rhys, Steven Yeun and Eddie Redmayne. THE ARC Hollywood has Orlando’s Central Florida Talent agency to thank for putting Buren on his path. After the New Jersey native graduated a semester early from nearby Rollins College, he picked up a gig at the model/talent agency to stay near friends who were still in school. Though he imagined he might become an engineer someday, he accepted an L.A.-based relative’s offer to live with her while giving Hollywood a try. As luck would have it, agenting stuck, and after a stint at Gersh, the avid golfer joined CAA in 2014. Today, the married rep is entrusted by actors including Josh Hartnett, Charlie Hunnam and Hannah Waddingham. Earlier this fall, client (and double Emmy winner) Rhys gave Buren a shout-out from the Emmy stage. MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Serving coffee to people in an order determined by seniority and annual earnings. It was my first introduction to the Hollywood hierarchy, and I learned very quickly that even caffeine has a pecking order.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Being on a call with 15 people to schedule another call with 15 people, only to discover that the one person who actually needed to be there wasn’t invited.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “Lorne Michaels. To have spent five decades at the intersection of comedy, culture, and discovering talent is pretty remarkable.” Winnie Carrillo Montiel, 35 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Amazon MGM, film executive, production & development LOGLINE Oversees films that range from bro-y actioners ( The Wrecking Crew ) to weepy love stories ( Honeymoon With Harry ). THE ARC Carrillo Montiel’s career in entertainment began with a clerical error. As an Emerson undergrad, she was mistakenly admitted as a screenwriting major instead of the literature and publishing program she had applied to. She ended up staying the course, eventually doubling down by attending graduate school at USC’s famed Peter Stark Producing Program. While there, she landed a temp job in MGM’s film group, which she did by day, leaving classes for night. Ultimately, it was the studio’s then-president Jonathan Glickman who helped push through the Guatemala City native’s visa sponsorship to land her her first full-time Hollywood gig. “He just made me promise that I wouldn’t get my green card and leave,” she remembers. “This was almost a decade ago and I’m still here. So, I really kept my promise.” Carrillo Montiel has since survived several regime changes, not to mention an acquisition, to land at her current spot on Amazon MGM’s film team, where she has overseen such films as The Sheep Detectives and an upcoming slate with projects from Dan Fogelman ( Honeymoon ) and Michael Showalter (a Serendipity reimagining). One of her proudest accomplishments is shepherding Angel Manuel Soto’s The Wrecking Crew , explaining, “Latinos are often put in a very specific box, and we are only hired to tell Latino-specific stories. I’m always looking for opportunities to elevate talent that I think are just great filmmakers.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Unlimited budgets.” WORST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “I was advised to look for an American husband as I was told it would be impossible for me to earn a work visa in this industry.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Cold calling very specific animal experts in Russia and Brazil to attempt to track down recent sightings of extremely large species of bears and snakes.” Margaret Clark, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion 20th Television, director of development LOGLINE Manages a roster of overall deals (Liz Meriwether, Drew Goddard) and development projects, including the Hulu hit Furious . THE ARC Technically speaking, Clark was discovered at the Panera on South Beverly Drive. At least, that’s where a guy from APA overheard her during an informational coffee with a fellow University of Virginia alum and offered to pass along her résumé to his agency mailroom. She was hired the following week. “I treated it like my grad school,” Clark says of her agency stint. By late 2017, the Virginia native and onetime theater kid had jumped to 20th Television, where she eventually found her way to Dana Walden’s desk for three pivotal years. In that time, she gained both a high-level education and a top-tier mentor. These days, Clark’s back on the 20th team, punching above her weight as she manages a slate of projects and the studio’s IP pipeline. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jennifer Lopez in The Wedding Planner .” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Buying a single old-fashioned donut for the CEO on Friday mornings. It had to be from Winchell’s. I wasn’t his assistant.” THE BEST PLACE FOR A COFFEE MEETING IS “The National Theater in London. Or the ABC Riverside Starbucks.” Sarah Colvin, 30 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Neon, VP acquisitions LOGLINE Keeps Neon supplied with art house favorites and horror standouts, including The Secret Agent , Leviticus and All of a Sudden . THE ARC Colvin spends a good chunk of her year traveling to Sundance, Berlin, SXSW, Cannes and beyond in the name of supplying Neon’s film slate with titles that will soon be Letterboxd’s new obsession (see: Oliver Laxe’s Sirāt and the long-awaited doc Once Upon a Time in Harlem ). Raised in New Mexico by artist parents, young Colvin would spend whatever free time she had with friends at Santa Fe’s one art house cinema. She laughs, “We thought we were so highbrow.” But she took that passion to NYU, where her professor, indie producer David Hinojosa, helped her land an internship at Neon, right as the then-upstart distributor was releasing its first success, I, Tonya . “There was no formal end date to the internship,” she says. “Eventually, Tom [Quinn] was like, ‘You should probably have a job here, then.’ ” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A blend of PeeWee Herman and Griffin Mill from The Player .” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Wile E Coyote.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The great equalizer that is the valet stand after the Academy Awards.” Dylan Conklin, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Entertainment 360, manager LOGLINE Guides the careers of clients like Kaia Gerber and Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story star Ella Beatty. THE ARC Conklin was studying international business in China for a summer when he realized the path wasn’t for him. Fortunately, a TV class with guests from Breaking Bad and Mad Men opened his eyes to a career in the entertainment field instead. Following a stint as an assistant to producer Tripp Vinson and some good advice from mentor attorney Howard Weitzman, he landed at 360 in 2016. A decade later, the dad of two has an impressive roster of talent clients, including Costa D’Angelo, for whom he’s lined up back-to-back shows ( East of Eden , The Sticks , We Were Liars ), and Ji-young Yoo, whose post- KPop Demon Hunters path includes a Paramount movie and Presumed Innocent season two. BEST ADVICE ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Don’t chase hits. Champion exceptional artists, nurture their talent, and the hits will follow.” IT WAS FROM… “Mo Ostin.” THE TALENT I’D KILL TO WORK WITH IS “Danny DeVito.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “Making PB&J sandwiches in the office kitchen with Jennifer Garner.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH “Jerry Bruckheimer.” Kai Dolbashian, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion 1.21, Film & TV development head LOGLINE Identified filmmaker Michael Shanks and helped develop Together from script to splashy Sundance sale. THE ARC While attending Chapman’s film school, Dolbashian landed an internship at MGM TV. The problem: The job was an hour away on a good day, and he had no car. Though he racked up credit card bills renting Zipcars, the bet paid off. He scored a post-grad gig and found a mentor in producer Andrew Mittman. And when Mittman launched his own banner in 2020, he was there on day one. Now, as the company’s head of film and TV development, Dolbashian has a slew of projects in development, including Warner Bros.’ remake of Attack of the 50 Foot Woman with Margot Robbie and Tim Burton. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Arno from Uncut Gems . We’re both impatient Armenians and both desperately want to do business with Adam Sandler.” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “The first time I had lunch with Christoph Waltz, he cut and ate his strudel exactly the way his infamous character Hans Landa does in Inglourious Basterds . Thankfully, unlike Hans, Christoph is one of the nicest human beings.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Bill Hader. There is literally no one else who could write and direct that epic motorcycle chase and shootout from season three of Barry , yet also perfectly embody the unhinged role of Officer Slater in Superbad. ” Carly Elter, 32 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Hidden Pictures, senior vp film and TV LOGLINE The architect behind The Housemaid is also behind lit-centric packages based on best-sellers from Rebecca Yarros and V. E. Schwab. THE ARC When Elter first walked into the house at the center of her 2025 movie The Housemaid , she cried. “It was such a surreal moment,” she says. “In my apartment, I read a book that I thought was a good idea for a movie, and now we have 100 people-plus employed making that movie.” Elter sold the film adaptation when it was self-published by author Freida McFadden; it would later land a publishing deal and sell 6 million copies, while the movie earned more than $400 million and quickly scored a sequel, which is in production. When she’s not on set, you can find her taking coffee meetings at her climbing gym, doing karaoke in Koreatown or traveling the world with her partner. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Calvin from Calvin and Hobbes .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Teleportation powers, so that I can be on set and sleep in my own bed.” Alix Taylor, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Gloria Sanchez, head of TV LOGLINE Oversees a slate of nearly a dozen upcoming projects, including adaptations of Dream State and Prep . THE ARC Raised two blocks from her public library in Atlanta, Taylor was a self-proclaimed “psychotic reader.” In fact, she says, “We’d joke that when my mom was working, she’d drop me there and that was my day care.” Fittingly, she became a comparative literature major at Brown, though Taylor thought she, like her mom, would ultimately pursue a career in the art world. There were a few internships and early gigs, but in the end, Hollywood proved more alluring. After a quick stint with producer Nathan Kahane, Taylor found her way to Amazon’s comedy team, where she worked on series like Undone , Modern Love and Overcompensating before jumping to Will Ferrell’s company to run the TV division three and a half years ago. She’s since built a considerable slate, with projects in various stages of development, including several adaptations and one idea loosely inspired by Taylor’s time interning at Christie’s. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Jane from Broadcast News — but not in a depressing way.” MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Spending every Friday afternoon at my boss’ house turning on and off all the lights to check for burned-out bulbs.” IF I HAD A ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH FOR … “Dramaturgically, this feels like a trap.” Christian Vazquez, 30 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Indie producer LOGLINE Lance Oppenheim’s right hand on You Can See Everything and Primetime . THE ARC If you were a firefighter in the mid-aughts and flashed your badge at Long Beach’s Regal movie theater, they’d usher you in for free. Such was the experience of Vazquez and his two siblings thanks to their firefighter dad, an immigrant from Mexico. Vazquez was a driven student and track athlete, and ultimately made his way to Harvard, where he met Oppenheim, who asked for his help producing his senior thesis film. That film became the Sundance darling Some Kind of Heaven , about the Villages retirement community in Florida. Spermworld and the HBO docuseries Ren Faire followed, but nothing compares to this year’s Elizabeth Holmes doc, a box office hit and an Oscar contender. The latter came just weeks after their first narrative feature, the Robert Pattinson starrer Primetime . Vazquez, a hands-on producer who never misses a day on set, has been out of town working on HBO’s Neighbors for the rollout of both films. His firefighter dad (now retired) has attended the premieres in his place, and has been introducing himself to talent, including Nathan Fielder. TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Danny McBride.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “Never ask someone to do something you wouldn’t do yourself.” FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Shelley ‘The Machine’ Levene.” Allie Veneris, 34 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Brillstein, manager LOGLINE Navigating the careers of Cara Delevingne, whom she put in Club Kid , as well as Phil Dunster and Reacher spinoff star Maria Sten. THE ARC The Huntington Beach native grew up as a sports enthusiast who loved softball and golf. She studied film editing at Boulder before a friend suggested becoming a rep: “I was way too extroverted to be an editor,” she says with a laugh. The revelation led to an internship at Brillstein and then stints at Gersh, 360 and Authentic. Amid the strikes, she returned to Brillstein and has leaned into a personal passion for music and sports. The latter space fueled recent wins, like Sophie Nélisse booking Heated Rivalry a month after Veneris set up a general with creator Jacob Tierney. Ted Lasso breakout Dunster — Veneris’ frequent companion for Dodgers and Arsenal games — is not only joining the How to Train Your Dragon live-action franchise but has moved into writing and producing, as has longtime client Jessica Rothe, who leads the TIFF horror favorite River . Thanks to her obsession with online trends, Veneris jumped to work with gymnast-turned-content creator Livvy Dunne — making her acting debut on Fox’s Baywatch reboot — and would not rest until Cara Delevingne landed Club Kid , the Cannes sensation from former viral comedian Jordan Firstman. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “A mix of Liz Lemon ( 30 Rock ), Sutton Brady ( The Bold Type ) and Jimmy from Hacks .” IF I HAD ONE WISH WILLOW, I’D WISH … “To have the attention span of someone who has never heard of TikTok.” TALENT I’M DYING TO WORK WITH “Kristen Stewart … and any or all members of Blackpink.” Paige Wandling, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Range, manager LOGLINE Reps hot TV talent Shailene Woodley and Fallout ’s Ella Purnell. THE ARC A hostessing gig at a small Malibu restaurant gave Wandling her earliest brushes with Hollywood notables. “If I thought they could be someone, I would Google them,” she says. “Oh! That’s David Ellison. Oh my God, that’s Nicole Avant and Ted Sarandos.” The Pepperdine grad would have many more such brushes when she moved from ID PR to CAA, where she worked for David Bugliari, whom she’d later follow to Range. After getting a tip from an assistant friend that Woodley had parted ways with her manager, she spent the next year working sources for intel that could woo the actress. One such piece of intel paid off when she learned an actress had dropped out of Michael Mann’s Ferrari . Wandling helped coordinate a meeting between the actress and the filmmaker. Woodley got the part and signed with Range, with Wandling attending the Emmys this to watch her client win for Paradise . The Minneapolis native and former competitive dancer has also guided the careers of Purnell, Gabrielle Union and Furious star Lola Petticrew, who landed the co-lead in the upcoming Assassin’s Creed . MY FIRST JOB IN HOLLYWOOD ENTAILED … “Finding six dozen sunflowers the Saturday before Oscars Sunday for a client who wanted to decorate a fellow nominee’s hotel room with them.” BEST ADVICE I’VE GOTTEN ABOUT WORKING IN HOLLYWOOD “The most important thing about any job in representation is to ‘anticipate the need.'” IT WAS FROM … “Publicist Leah Chang.” Caroline Warner, 33 Image Credit: Photographed by Mark Griffin Champion Apple TV, domestic programming executive LOGLINE Supports some of the streamer’s most ambitious TV bets, from Ascension to Disclaimer . THE ARC “I’ve always been obsessed with TV,” says Warner, who received a script from Charmed for her 10th birthday. The New York native parlayed that passion into a series of internships — at Katie Couric’s short-lived talk show, Piers Morgan Live and at Showtime — while still at Yale and, later, a post-grad gig in the WME mailroom. But after a job at Chernin, she was debating a career pivot, beginning with business school. It was her dad who advised her to try one more gig before deciding. That job was at Apple TV+, where Warner was the fourth-ever hire. Rising through the ranks, she’s now working with Alfonso Cuarón for the second time on his upcoming series Ascension and, already mother to a rescue dog named Winston, is expecting her first child. FICTIONAL CHARACTER I MOST IDENTIFY WITH “Dream: Rory Gilmore. Reality: Paris Geller.” PERSON IN HOLLYWOOD I’D TRADE PLACES WITH FOR A DAY “I feel like this is a cliche but I’d be lying if I said anyone other than Jeff Probst!” MOST HOLLYWOOD EXPERIENCE I’VE HAD “I had to babysit a puppet for four days on my first business trip. It was awesome.” This story appears in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: ‘GTA 6’ vs. Hollywood: Industry Braces for “Biggest Entertainment Launch in History”
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Amazon MGM’s new season of 'Rings of Power' and Lionsgate's latest 'Hunger Games' installment are bowing right as 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is poised to dominate the entertainment landscape. Illustrated by Cat Sims Logo text Are gamers who have waited 13 years to return to Vice City really going to spend their time in Panem, Middle-earth, and the Underworld instead? The massively anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI , coming Nov. 19, will land amid a slew of expensive and high-profile movies and returning TV shows dropping within several days of each other. Most of them offer their own escapist fantasy worlds that will compete in the attention economy with a title that’s expected to be the biggest video game launch in history. Season three of Amazon-MGM’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is rolling out episodes over three weeks beginning Nov. 11 and Johnny Depp’s comeback vehicle Ebenezer lands Nov. 13. Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens the day after GTA 6 launches on Nov. 20 along with the fourth season of the studio’s Paramount+ hit Yellowjackets . The same day, Disney rolls out the third season of Percy Jackson and the Olympians . Five days down the road comes Amazon MGM’s limited series Blade Runner 2099 . “It’s going to be a watershed moment for not only the gaming industry but also all the folks in the media and entertainment industry who are going to have to deal with the fact that eyeballs are going to be leaving their environments to go play GTA 6 ,” said Bart Spiegel, global media, entertainment, gaming and sports leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers. It’s indeed tough to overstate the earthquake GTA6 is expected to create in terms of entertainment spending, distraction hours and pop culture noise. The Rockstar Games project has a first-year sales forecast of 45 million copies and $3.2 billion in sales — a figure which would top all-time box office champ Avengers: Endgame . A whopping 29 percent of U.S. gamers expect to purchase the title and one economist suggested, rather wildly, that the game would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion in lost productivity due to PTO requests. Other video game publishers have run for the hills and surrendered November to Rockstar’s sun-drenched, pastel-colored 800-pound gorilla. “I think GTA 6 will be the biggest entertainment launch in history,” predicts Geoff Keighley, gaming industry producer and entrepreneur behind The Game Awards . “Not just as a game in terms of dollars it will make — this will easily trump Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three — but how much it will impact moviegoing, streaming, and the way people spend their time. Hollywood should look at the hours as closely as the dollars because GTA 6 is going to be some people’s entertainment plan for the rest of the year, basically. The entertainment industry has never really seen something like this before.” While the game’s core mission will likely take around 80 hours to complete — which alone is a massive amount of hours for one title — the title is also an open world environment where players tend to return again and again, and insiders assume the game will allow some kind of online multiplayer mode as well. “So this is not just about opening weekend,” Keighley says. But for Hollywood, which is accustomed to largely owning the entertainment attention economy, particularly around the holidays, the impact of GTA 6 seems almost certainly to be felt — if difficult to measure. Spiegel noted streaming is likely to take the biggest hit because a console game directly competes for viewing hours on living room TVs. Last year’s fourth quarter streaming numbers were rather strong, he noted, but he suspects GTA 6 could put a real dent in the year-over-year comps. The live urgency of sports viewing, however, will be safer from erosion than entertainment programming. “But trust me, if that game gets boring, GTA 6 is going on pretty soon,” he quipped. Behind the scenes, streamers are increasingly aware GTA 6 is coming and that Jason and Lucia might rob some of their viewers. “Everybody is rumbling about how big this game is going to be,” says a representative working with one potentially impacted streaming title. On the film side, a major exhibitor executive said it’s “tough to know” the effect on films like Ebenezer and Sunrise on the Reaping. “ It’s hardly come up in internal discussions, but anyone in the industry who’s ever been a gamer — or who lives with someone who is — knows it’ll have some impact,” he said. “Hunger Games presales are strong, which might point to it being solid counter programming. Ebenezer presales are dire, but I doubt GTA6 is the main reason. We’ll have to see how walkup sales go.” Future box office heavy hitters like Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three , which open “Dunesday” Dec. 18. Such titles would seem to fall outside the game’s blast radius, but perhaps not. Spiegel has noted the game’s “pull could last through December.” While hardcore gamers will rush out and play GTA 6 the first few weeks, others will hold off until they have more free time during the December holidays, while some kids (with rather permissive parents) won’t even be unwrapping the presumably Mature-rated game until Christmas. Music will be disrupted, too, with the game’s 34-song soundtrack already at 26 million monthly listens on Spotify and a 30-track original score by Justice coming Dec. 11. One as-yet-unappreciated aspect of the game’s gravitational pull will be on social media, where you’re already starting to see anticipatory videos (such as a boyfriend getting his girlfriend a kitten so she won’t bother him while playing the game, or another boyfriend who seemingly wrote up a contract pledging a list of compromises if his girlfriend doesn’t, yes, bother him while playing the game). But social media is also massive part of entertainment marketing — not just direct advertising but fan-generated content that helps programs generate buzz and become part of the cultural conversation. But what happens if GTA 6 becomes all anybody is talking about? “It’s going to take over live streaming and clips and content creators,” Keighley says. “Barbenheimer worked because you could go see Barbie and Oppenheimer , and you only needed five or six hours. People will still go see other things, but I think the entertainment value has to be extremely high.” This story appeared in the Nov. 12 issue of The Hollywood Reporter magazine.

title: ‘Tangled’ Takes Ciudad de la Luz From Up-and-Coming Studio to Production Must-Stop
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The morning sun hits Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity For the team at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, 2026 is the year it went from an up-and-coming shoot destination to a top-tier must-stop for major international productions. In Alicante, this large-scale film and TV hub was born from the vision of Spanish filmmaker and screenwriter Luis García Berlanga, who in 2005 set out to reindustrialize the Spanish audiovisual sector. That initial seven-year phase culminated in 63 projects, including J.A. Bayona’s The Impossible and Francis Ford Coppola’s Tetro . Studio Ciudad de la Luz reopened in 2023 with a renewed intention to set itself apart from its rivals. Boasting state-of-the-art facilities, it has six climate-controlled stages, interconnected in pairs, and two indoor, floodable pits that come in at over three metres deep. Among its signature draws is the outdoor water tank, a 100-by-80-meter facility with wave-generation systems, water cannons, slides, a seawater pumping system and partial fill-and-drain capability. The backlot totals 14.8 hectares of space with natural horizon, power, water and telecommunications, over 4,000 square meters of workshop space and 7,000 square meters of storage space, with three production support buildings hosting dressing rooms, make-up, hair, offices and services. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM And from 2023 to 2025, this production eden was a well-kept secret. Among some of their projects during that time period were Venom: The Last Dance with Tom Hardy, generating 35 million euros and 570 contracts, as well as The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon , which shot in the aforementioned water tank, the French Netflix shows Nero and Under Paris , as well as Alberto Rodriguez’ Los Tigres and Alejandro Amenabar’s El Cautivo , which had an estimated economic impact of eight million Euros. But the word is officially out. This year, the studio has found industry consolidation in two projects of significant scale: Disney’s live-action Tangled and the permanent establishment of The Good Film Studios Spain , helping Ciudad de la Luz absorb some of the most technically and logistically demanding shoots with newfound confidence. Ciudad de la Luz is currently the only facility in Europe that allows indoor, outdoor and aquatic filming on the same site. That kind of versatility — paired with a warm-weather climate, competitive incentives and an experienced local crew — is attracting the eyeballs of producers across the globe. A shot from the outdoor water tank at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Publicity Michael Gracey’s Tangled , produced by Kristin Burr, has emerged as a case-in-point example of what’s possible at this production behemoth. The original 2010 animation, following Rapunzel’s team-up with a local outlaw, the devilish Flynn Rider, was a smash hit that swiftly accrued nearly $600 million at the global box office. Set for a 2028 theatrical release and starring Teagan Croft, Milo Manheim and Kathryn Hahn, the new era of Tangled was shot at Studio Ciudad de la Luz over 10 months from February to October this year and involved the intensive use of stages, on-site exteriors and locations across the region of Valencia. Its direct economic impact on Ciudad de la Luz is currently over 40 million euros, with more than 1,000 professionals mobilized on the project. A whopping 2,500 local contracts were generated by the arrival of this Hollywood production, lending help to the studio’s 90 percent occupancy in 2026. Gracey argues that fellow U.S. execs should consider booking that flight to Alicante. “There’s an extraordinary level of passion and dedication here,” he says ahead of the American Film Market. “That energy comes across on screen.” The filmmaker, best known for his work on The Greatest Showman (2017) and Better Man (2024), said his crew was able to combine exterior and interior stages, “and it feels real,” he adds. “You don’t notice the transition.” He sings the praises of the local crews and scenery here in southeast Spain. The region certainly gives Los Angeles a run for its money, attracting more than 300 days of sunshine a year and diverse landscapes such as beaches, mountains, salt flats and protected natural areas. With the bustling Spanish town of Alicante, an international airport, and hotel capacity of over 70,000 beds in the surrounding area, Gracey lauds the no-fuss environment: “The people, the locations and the spaces have been fantastic. Having the city only 15 minutes away is a real advantage.” Burr even hails it as her “favorite location.” She explains: “The stages are among the most spectacular I’ve ever worked on [and] I’m extremely impressed by the level of dedication we’ve seen on the sets. I’m very demanding when it comes to production design, and I think this is some of the best I’ve seen in my career.” As vocal advocates of Studio Ciudad de la Luz, Gracey and Burr are in good company. Top producer Miriam Segal founded the Good Films Collective in 2007, established to develop and finance “intelligent, inclusive and commercially ambitious independent films.” Now, her joint venture with the Spanish government and Canadian-U.S. outfit Orogen Media, The Good Films Studios Spain has set up a permanent home at Studio Ciudad de la Luz, bringing with it an investment of 19.8 million Euros from the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT) and private partners. With the arrival of Segal’s Spanish branch here in Alicante — a long-term commitment eyeing 20 international features over the next 10 years — her company has evolved from rising production outfit to integrated studio business. “It’s the best crew I’ve worked with anywhere in the world,” says Segal, known for The Infiltrator (2016) with Bryan Cranston and The Postcard Killings (2020) with Jeffrey Dean Morgan. The Good Films Studios Spain have set their first film out of the Alicante hub: People of the Book , directed by Michael Haussman and based on the novel of the same name written by Pulitzer Prize-winning author Geraldine Brooks. The cast includes Ziad Bakri, Rania Ben Fattoum, Ankido Hussen, Luca Ferrini, Giorgia Sinicorni, Pasquale Esposito and Jose Luis Ferrier, who filmed in the studio’s outdoor water tank, as well as on their stages and workshops. It isn’t just the expansive facilities drawing the industry’s most prolific producers and crews, but the territory’s expertly trained ecosystem of graduates. The Film Trades School initiative, developed in collaboration with the country’s leading film school, Escola Superior de Cinema i Audiovisuals de Catalunya (ESCAC), has upskilled thousands of students across more than 30 specialisms, including set construction, lighting, camera, sound, VFX, green filming, costume, production, who are able to come and hone their craft at Studio Ciudad de la Luz. Regional and national tax incentives continue to be a real weapon in the team’s arsenal. A non-repayable grant of 25 percent on production and post-production expenditure is available in Valencia for a maximum relief of 1.5 million Euros per project. At the country-wide level, Spanish productions and co-productions can claim 30 percent of the first million and 25 percent on the remainder back, capped at 20 million Euros per production. For foreign shoots in Spain, it’s the exact same, but the minimum spend in the country must total at least one million Euros. Ciudad de la Luz and the region of Valencia are hopeful they’ve consolidated their position as a real and competitive option in the league of Europe’s most demanding production destinations. And the knock-on effect so far is palpable: “When the Region of Valencia believes in itself,” begins Marián Cano, the regional minister for industry, tourism, innovation and trade, “it can compete with anyone to attract top-level projects.” THR

title: ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: Nicholas Hoult Delivers Adrenalized Big Finance Payback That Entertains Despite Its Tonal Mishmash
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicholas Hoult in 'How to Rob a Bank.' Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios If the midterm elections were not indication enough that Americans are feeling the pinch and hitting back at a system heavily rigged to favor obscene wealth and unchecked power, high-octane action specialist David Leitch ’s How to Rob a Bank offers further evidence. A kinetic heist thriller in which we root for the thieves — Mark Bianculli’s script name-checks Point Break , swapping Ex-Presidents for animal masks — the good-looking movie doesn’t reconcile its twin identities as a crime caper with a satirical edge and a poignant social justice fantasy. But a strong ensemble keeps things moving. Related Stories Movies David Leitch's 'How to Rob a Bank': First Reactions Movies How David Leitch Made 'How to Rob a Bank' on a Budget -- and Around Nicholas Hoult's Torn ACL Following up on the breezy insouciance of The Fall Guy , Leitch directs with his foot planted firmly on the accelerator, reassembling his trusty core team of DP Jonathan Sela, production designer David Scheunemann, composer Dom Lewis and editor Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir. If the early action overloads on YouTube interface and quippy content creation, that’s amply justified in the script, though it’s a relief when the movie takes time to breathe and allow the characters some depth. How to Rob a Bank The Bottom Line Now is the winter of our collective discontent. Release date : Friday, Nov. 13 Cast : Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, John C. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director : David Leitch Screenwriter : Mark Bianculli Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes Nicholas Hoult plays underdog antihero Ryan, aka “The Wolf,” who leads a close-knit crew of Pittsburgh bank robbers and fronts their popular online videos in a furry lupine mask. “Content is king,” he says in voiceover narration, explaining that an audience is more powerful than a gun. Their YouTube show is widely known by the acronym HTRAB and the catchphrase, “Who’s hungry?” It plays not only tightly edited footage of their daring bank escapades, providing tips for a growing number of copycat robbers across the country, but also their “pay it forward” philosophy of tossing cash at bank employees and customers, distributing larger sums to charities like schools, churches and hospitals. At a time when the American Dream is accessible only to the top wealth bracket, these bad guys are good guys, and they make it look easy. Says Ryan: “You’re more likely to live your entire life under the poverty line than get caught stealing your way out from under it.” The HTRAB crew includes Ryan’s partner Emi ( Anna Sawai ), the getaway driver and strategist, an expert at creating diversions to keep law enforcement occupied; combat vet Vince ( Pete Davidson ), who found that after he fought for his country in Afghanistan, his VA health insurance was not prepared to fight for him the same way; and tech wizard Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), who shapes the YouTube content. Like many of their millions of followers — burdened by student debt and shrinking job opportunities, the goal of home ownership and medical coverage remaining out of reach — Ryan & Co. share a common bond of having run out of options. Bankrupted by medical bills and predatory money-lending policies, he and Emi struggle to accept tragedy that might have been forestalled with more available means. Hugo and Vince, who’s up against a ticking clock, are just desperate to provide for their families. While the robberies are diverting enough and the YouTube inserts splashed with pop-up graphics, the fun wears a bit thin, which makes the shift into trauma and pathos a welcome one, even if the transition might have been smoother. Basically, it turns into a different movie. The cast compensates for any shortage of fluidity, however, notably Hoult and Sawai, whose sexy body language counters the lacerating sorrow and anger left by a devastating loss; and Davidson, who curbs his comedy instincts to show uncustomary shadings. His final scene in the movie is intensely moving, in what’s arguably the actor’s best performance since The King of Staten Island . Feliz, best known for Marvel’s Runaways and HBO’s The Penguin , is given less to do, but his sparky personality makes him a magnetic presence. Having pulled off 15 bank robberies over three months and triggered a 400 percent increase in similar operations nationwide, the HTRAB bandits remain frustratingly elusive to the FBI. Nearing retirement and unwilling to go out on a failure, veteran agent John West ( John C. Reilly ) refuses to accept his team’s lack of leads. He recruits coding genius Reagan (Zoë Kravitz) to examine the hours of YouTube material for clues and patterns. An associate professor at Carnegie Mellon, Reagan is now serving time under house arrest on a hacking charge. She’s resistant at first, reluctant to break her routine of bong hits and junk food, not to mention sympathetic to the robbers’ cause. But West wins her over with an exchange that will wipe her slate clean. Reagan is a very cool character who gives Kravitz plenty of room to inject sly humor and irreverent attitude, even just via the low-key running joke of her constant eating in every scene. Initially looking to hunt down a deadbeat ex-boyfriend, she developed a tracking program called FYPOS (“Fuck You Piece of Shit”) designed to locate people via their social media activity. That becomes an essential tool in the FBI investigation. But after giving Reagan an intriguing setup, Bianculli’s script runs out of ideas for the character, relegating her to observer status for much of the climactic stretch. Reilly is put to better use as an old-school agency man set on doing his job, but with enough misfortune behind him to understand what drives Ryan and his crew. The chaotically plotted penultimate act involves West closing in during the “big finish” that the HTRAB team have been carefully plotting for months. That involves their agenda getting personal as they hit heavyweight financial institution Vitality Trust. That monolith is run by David Walton (Christian Slater), an arrogant asshole whose merciless loan scheme was designed to reap huge profits once the borrowers had been bled dry. The volatile mob of HTRAB followers gathered in the blocks surrounding VT inevitably recalls the wealth inequality protests of 2011 that began near Wall Street and spread to cities across the country, including Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Seattle. That brings a stirring “power to the people” sentiment, even as Ryan’s determination to complete their plan seems doomed once the Feds know their identities. But the movie keeps a few tricks up its sleeve for a satisfying coda. The narrative’s plot holes and contrivances don’t reward close inspection, but as an avenging underdog fairy tale pieced together from the shards of the American Dream, it’s fast-paced, entertaining and surprisingly emotional. That’s due in no small part to the soulful qualities the principals bring to their roles. Sela’s muscular camerawork, Lewis’ pulse-racing score and Ronaldsdóttir’s punchy editing all play vital parts, as do the energizing needle drops. These range from the pounding dubstep beats of “Victory Lap,” by Fred Again, Skepta and PlaqueBoyMax through the garage revival of The Hives, the alternative rock of Jane’s Addiction and the gorgeous, whispery vocals of Billie Eilish. The use of Radiohead’s haunting anti-corporate anthem “Karma Police” over one heartbreaking scene is a master stroke. How to Rob a Bank is not without flaws; there are times in the early action when it risks repeating the far-too-pleased-with-itself flashiness of Leitch’s numbing 2022 assault on the senses, Bullet Train . But there’s unexpected heart and a finger on the zeitgeist here that at least ensure it’s never dull — a mainstream commercial anti-capitalist movie in these rollercoaster times is a rare thing. Reilly, Christian Slater, Paul Sparks, Tati Gabrielle, Young Mazino, Alessandra Frugoli Director: David Leitch Screenwriter: Mark Bianculli Producers: Brian Grazer, Jeb Brody, Allan Mandelbaum, Kelly McCormick, David Leitch Executive producers: Ben Ormand, Mark Bianculli Director of photography: Jonathan Sela Production designer: David Scheunemann Costume designer: Jocelyn Pierce Music: Dom Lewis Editor: Elísabet Ronaldsdóttir Sound designers: Pat Haskill, Ryan Nowak, Gregorio Gomez Stunt designer: Greg Rementer Casting: Mary Vernieu, Lindsay Graham Ahanonu Rated R, 2 hours 2 minutes THR

title: Mind the Gap: British Producer-Financier Phil Hunt Is Bringing Head Gear Stateside
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 11, 2026 5:43am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Head Gear Co-founder and CEO Phil Hunt Phil Hunt, Hana Holmes The AFM got a welcome boost ahead of this year’s market when British producer-financier Head Gear unveiled plans to launch a U.S. operation, promising to invest $120 million in production in its first year of operation. Head Gear COO Samantha Allwinton will run the U.S. division as director of operations. For Phil Hunt , who launched Head Gear in 2002 with film financier (and oil industry exec) Compton Ross, setting up stateside has been a dream “for 25 years.” In the U.K., Head Gear has developed a reputation as the “producer’s producer,” working at every stage of financing and production — from presales and packaging to gap and bridge funding — to support about 30 films a year, including Talk to Me , Danny and Michael Philippou’s Australian horror breakthrough that grossed more than $90 million worldwide; Ali Abbasi’s Oscar-nominated “reality horror” film The Apprentice , about the making of Donald Trump ; and Molly Manning Walker’s art house crossover hit How to Have Sex. Related Stories Movies 'Exotic' Takes Us to Polish Pole Dance Camp to Tell a Female Story of Self-Discovery and Body Confidence Movies Producers Push for Year-End Passage of Trump-Backed Federal Film Incentive: AFM Head Gear also is active on the sales side through its international operation, Bankside Films, whose AFM slate this year includes the AI-themed sci-fi comedy Almost You , starring Juno Temple, Joey King and James McAvoy from Ted Lasso director Matt Lipsey. Bankside is selling the project, now shooting in Scotland, worldwide, co-repping the U.K. and North America with UTA Independent Film Group. Speaking with THR ahead of the market, Hunt explains why he’s bullish about the U.S., with or without a federal tax credit, the impact of the creator economy on indie film and what he’s learned from taking on Trump – and Julie Andrews . Why Head Gear USA, and how will it work? I’ve wanted a U.S. business for about 25 years. It took that long to find the right person to run it. Now the timing is right as well: more U.S. producers need financing, and a federal tax credit could bring a lot more production into the country. We’re putting about $120 million into U.S. film and TV in the first year. We’re not just a lender. We help producers package the project, build the financing plan, handle the business affairs and collect the money after release. We behave like a small studio. We decide whether a film goes into production, and we deliver about 35 films a year to our regular sales agents and buyers. Whether we like it or not, the U.S. leads the rest of the world on global distribution of English-speaking movies. Being there is often not an option. But we’re a British company with the culture we have built over the past quarter of a century, and that means we uphold key principles. We’re transparent and do what we say we’re going to do — while bringing a great punk rock style. ‘Talk to Me,’ which Head Gear backed, was a breakout hit, earning more than $90 million worldwide. Matthew Thorne/A24 How does the federal tax credit fit into your U.S. expansion plans, and what if it doesn’t pass? If it passes, a U.S. production gets cheaper to make and lenders can borrow against the credit, the way we already do in the U.K. and Europe. That’s why we’re setting up now, so we’re ready the day it lands. If it doesn’t pass, we’re still going to be investing heavily in U.S. movies. Nothing much changes that desire to open up there for the past 25 years. What are the biggest lessons you take from the past year’s indie successes and failures? The films that worked were made for a price that makes sense; good cast, clear idea, a budget the market can pay back. The ones that failed mostly cost too much for what they were. People priced the film on hope, not on what buyers actually pay. Second lesson: The old safety nets are gone. Revenue is down and costs are up. If your plan only works when everything goes right, it won’t work. Third: Be honest early. When a producer tells us the problem on day one, we can usually solve it together. Those are the people we make films with again and again. What has been the biggest disruption in traditional indie financing, and how has that changed how you put projects together? Presales stopped covering what they used to. Streamers buy fewer films from independents and pay less for the ones they do buy. So there’s a bigger gap between what a film costs and what’s guaranteed up front. Gap is the new equity. Investors like us now fill part of what used to be covered by sales. That means we build the film around the money from the start. We look at cast, genre and budget together, before the script is locked. We stay with low-cost, high-concept projects: action, thriller, horror. We also watch how much we have riding on any one genre or sales agent at a time. Head Gear scored a cross-over arthouse hit with ‘How to Have Sex’ from Molly Manning Walker Courtesy MUBI mk2 Films/Nikos Nikolopoulos How was Almost You financed? It’s a mix. Tax credit money from the U.K., a lender borrowing against it [us], some money from sales to territories, and equity from the producers and partners. Bankside came on early with the cast, which helped make the sales numbers believable. How is the creator economy affecting indie film? Creators have something indie films have always struggled to buy: an audience that already knows them. That matters more than ever because marketing a small film is hard and expensive. A creator with millions of followers brings people before the film is released. But a big following doesn’t automatically turn into cinema tickets. Watching a free video is very different from paying to see a film. The ones who will make it work are the creators who treat a film like a real production: proper script, proper budget, proper distribution plan. I’m interested in that. I’m not interested in a follower count on its own. But most of all it’s about great storytellers, whether they are from the creator economy or not. What’s been the biggest surprise for you, and which title (whatever the commercial success) are you most proud of? There’s a lot that I’m surprised that failed so badly, but on a more positive note: from a commercial perspective, it’s got to be Talk to Me . No one knew that it was going to do the incredible business it did. It changed global strategies for many distribution companies. On a more controversial note, it’s got to be The Apprentice , which talked to me in many ways. I’m always fascinated at the power movies can have globally. It was really the story of Frankenstein, how a monster was made. It’s the original horror — Trump is Frankenstein. It was almost “reality horror.” We got a cease and desist from Trump on the day of the film’s world premiere in Cannes, and of course we threw it in the bin … The way all the filmmakers went about making and releasing it is truly punk rock. Sebastian Stan as Donald Trump in ‘The Apprentice.’ Pief Weyman/Rich Spirit What project did you learn the most from, in terms of your approach to the business? It’s got to be my second feature, Chunky Monkey , which I made in 2000 in the early days of my producing career. The great Greg Cruttwell wrote and directed it, and I was the sole producer — in the days when there was only one producer credit. Some folk called it a cult movie, others were disgusted by it. [The comedy features, among other things, a Julie Andrews-lookalike prostitute and the obscene use of Chunky Monkey ice cream.] Particularly offended were Rogers & Hammerstein, EMI, Julie Andrews, Unilever and the original creator of the Chunky Monkey comic strip [Pauline Comanor], all of whom tried to sue us and totally failed. [Comanor] claimed Ben & Jerry stole the name from her. Unilever, who bought the ice cream manufacturers, were incensed about the nature of our depiction of “finding another pleasurable” use for the ice cream. EMI was being forced by the very conservative Rogers and Hammerstein [estate] to withdraw its signed agreement with us. We rerecorded “The Hills Are Alive With the Sound of Music” with our Black Jesus singing and the pink panther playing the bongos. Julie Andrews just didn’t get our love note to her … I got more column inches over the period of a month than any studio movie. It was a David and Goliath story that stole the front page of many newspapers. The film was harmless, and it just shows you how people react without really reviewing the facts. While the film made no money, it was pirated a lot and got a cult following and put me on the map as a producer. I made sure everyone in the industry knew me after that. I realized then this business is all about marketing.” THR

title: Judge Declines To Dismiss Donald Trump’s Defamation Claim Against BBC
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Judge Declines To Dismiss Donald Trump’s Defamation Claim Against BBC House Blocks Effort To Impeach Secretary Of Defense Pete Hegseth Pete Hegseth Defends Tenure, Lavishes Praise On Trump & Calls Impeachment Threat “Sabotage” In Rare Pentagon Press Conference View All November 10, 2026 6:06pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source (L-R) Donald Trump & the BBC headquarters in London Getty A federal judge on Tuesday declined to dismiss Donald Trump ‘s defamation claim against the BBC over edits made to a documentary about January 6th that aired in advance of the 2024 election. U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz rejected the BBC’s efforts to toss the case, ruling that Trump had sufficiently pleaded actual malice. In his ruling, Kuntz wrote that the BBC confirmed “it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made. And it acknowledged it chose to release the video in a documentary only a week before the 2024 Presidential Election, at the time it would have the most impact. To make sure it was seen in Florida, BBC even emailed U.S. and Florida based commenters with instructions to on how to view the documentary.” Related Stories News Netflix's 'The Perfect Neighbor' Beats 'Mr Nobody Against Putin' To Top Prize At UK Grierson Documentary Awards Legal Hasan Piker's $72.5M Defamation Suit Over Lynching Quotes Should Be Tossed Out, Scott Jennings Says; Statements Are "Literally True," CNN Contributor Claims He added, “Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day.” Watch on Deadline The judge kept alive Trump’s defamation claim but dismissed his claim of violation of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion. In the documentary, Trump: A Second Chance? , a clip is shown from his January 6 speech, in which he says, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol … and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” In fact, the remark was an edit of different portions of the speech. Trump claims that the documentary — which was produced by October Films — was streamed on iPlayer by “hundreds of individuals” using a VPN in the U.S., despite it being geoblocked in America. His lawyers have accused the BBC of a “brazen” attempt to interfere in the 2024 U.S. election, which the corporation denies. In the fallout from edited speech, BBC director general Tim Davie and Deborah Turness , who led the news division, stepped down. The BBC apologized, calling it an “error of judgment,” but they did not offer to pay any damages. The judge wrote of the editing, “Trump properly alleges that BBC spliced and edited together a twelve-second segment that resulted in reputational harm based off ‘deceptive and defamatory distortion.'” “On its face, a twelve-second clip seems insignificant, but in the context of the complaint, these twelve seconds are the result of splicing two segments that are separated by nearly fifty-five minutes in the speech from which the segment is sourced.” Among other things, the BBC contended that Trump lacked personal jurisdiction, as the Panorama documentary did not air in Florida, where the case was filed. The judge ruled that Trump had sufficiently claimed jurisdiction. The judge wrote, “Trump has alleged extensive contacts tying BBC to the State of Florida. BBC tries to frame this as an operation entirely disconnected from Florida. That cannot be the case. Trump is a Florida resident, and the Documentary is almost entirely about Trump. Portions were filmed in Florida and BBC identified Florida as an important part of the Documentary. Therefore, ‘it seems disingenuous’ for BBC to argue that they ‘could not have anticipated being haled into court in Florida.'” Kuntz was nominated to the bench by Trump and confirmed by the Senate earlier this year. Trump called the ruling a “huge victory” and called the BBC “a terrible abuser of truth.” He wrote on Truth Social, “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” A BBC spokesperson said, “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. “We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process. It would be inappropriate to comment further while proceedings are ongoing.” Sarandos Faces Unrest From Past & Present Execs Over Netflix’s Direction ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Film & Stage Actor, Dies At 85; Career In Photos Jason Orley Directing New Take On Rom-Com ‘You’ve Got Mail’ For Warner Bros Leah McKendrick Sets ‘Voicemails From Isabelle’ Follow-Up; Maddie Ziegler Stars Read More About: 7 Comments

This post contains details from the Season 35 Dancing with the Stars quarterfinals. It’s hard to believe Dancing with the Stars Season 35 is nearly over, but we’ve officially reached the quarterfinals. There are seven couples remaining, but only five can make it all the way to the finale later this month. One couple is facing elimination on Grammy night, where the contestants will be performing to some of the biggest hits in music from artists including Evanescence, Sisqó, Beyoncé, Janet Jackson and more. Related Stories News Luke Bryan, Megan Moroney & Vince Gill Among Performers Added To CMA Awards News Former 'DWTS' Contestant Danielle Fishel Says Judges Tougher On Female Contestants: "Men Get A Pass" For the second week in a row, the couples are performing a second dance on Tuesday night. This week, they’re going toe-to-toe for the dance off, which pits two couples directly against each other to a live accompaniment. The pairings are as follows: Amber vs. Ezra, Jenna vs. Tatyana and Connor vs. Maura. Watch on Deadline After earning immunity with the highest cumulative score to-date last week, Harry and Jenna will sit out of the dance off. Sheryl Crow, Brandy and Monica, and Maren Morris will join the stage to perform some of their hit songs for the head-to-head competition. Let’s get into it. INDIVIDUAL DANCES Paralympian Ezra Frech with Daniella Karagach . These two were in a flow state last week, and after earning a 10 from Derek for their Disney Night performance, they’re taking on an Argentine tango to “Crazy in Love (Remix)” by Beyoncé for Grammy Night. SCORE: 27 out of 30 Olympian Amber Glenn with Pasha Pashkov . As if she hasn’t already, Amber says she really wants to show off her inner athlete on the ballroom floor this week with a paso doble to to “Bring Me to Life” by Evanescence. SCORE: 28 out of 30 Reality star Maura Higgins with Mark Ballas . After barely escaping elimination last week, Maura is putting all her focus into an Argentine tango to “Thong Song” by Sisqó. She’s working through some pain in her rib, so that’s proving to be a challenge in rehearsals, but she pushes the pain aside and delivers a performance that Carrie Ann calls “a work of art.” SCORE: 27 out of 30 Actress Jenna Dewan with Val Chmerkovskiy . She got a perfect score last week, so Jenna is riding high and ready to take on a jazz routine to “All For You” by Janet Jackson. She previously performed at the Grammys, so she’s also got to stake her claim when walking on the floor Tuesday night. SCORE: Actress Tatyana Ali with Jan Ravnik . This Fresh Prince star has been friends with Will.I.Am for more than two decades, so she much do justice to a tango to “Boom Boom Pow” by Black Eyed Peas. She’s got to nail the sharpness of this choreography in order to wow the judges. SCORE: Comedian and podcaster Connor Wood with Rylee Arnold . Based on the comments from the judges last week, he’s got to take the lead if he wants to impress them tonight with an Argentine tango to “SexyBack” by Justin Timberlake featuring Timbaland. Now, if only he could stay on his axis point, as Carrie Ann points out. SCORE: 27 out of 30 Actor Harry Shum Jr. with Jenna Johnson . Harry says he’s avoiding doing salsa dancing for so long because it reminds him of a hard time in his childhood, so dancing a salsa to “Die with A Smile” by Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars is bringing up a lot of emotions for him. SCORE: 29 out of 30 DANCE OFF Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov vs. Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach competed in a Rumba to “The Boy Is Mine” by Brandy and Monica. WINNER: Amber & Pasha (+2 bonus points) Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy vs. Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik faced off in a Cha-Cha to “The Middle” by Zedd, Maren Morris and Grey. WINNER: Jenna and Val (+2 bonus points) Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold vs. Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas . will compete in a Cha-Cha to “All I Wanna Do” by Sheryl Crow. title: ITV Cutting $40M From Media & Entertainment Budget Due To Weak Advertising Market
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max How The ‘Married At First Sight UK’ Scandal Has Impacted Hit Show Around The World Jonathan Ross Explains Backstory Behind “Tasteless” David Walliams Joke ITV Cutting $40M From Media & Entertainment Budget Due To Weak Advertising Market View All November 11, 2026 12:59am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Love Island's Maya Jama ITV2 With “weaker demand for advertising” in Q4, ITV has identified £30M ($40M) worth of cost savings from its networks division, which will soon be sold to Sky . Total Advertising Revenue is set to drop 5-10% in Q4 and 2-3% for full year 2026, ITV said today in its Q3 trading update. The network is therefore finding savings from its Media & Entertainment biz, which houses the ITV network and streamer ITVX, “to align our costs with advertiser demand.” ITV said £25M will come from content savings and another £5M from “discretionary non-content savings,” with the total content budget for 2026 now expected to be around £1.2B. Related Stories News 'Britain's Got Talent' Producer Urges "Anyone Who Feels They Have Been Subject Of Wrongdoing" To Come Forward Following David Walliams Allegations News ITV News & Guardian Closer To Publishing Sexual Misconduct Allegations About British Star After Injunction Appeal Deadline Passed ITV boss Carolyn McCall put the sticky ad market down to “continuing broader macroeconomic uncertainty, increased digital advertising on global streaming platforms and the impact of Less Healthy Food regulations, which came into effect on 1 October 2025.” Watch on Deadline ITV revealed a similar saving target last year due to a “softening economy” in the UK. The news comes as Comcast-owned Sky pushes on with its £1.6B acquisition of ITV, although as revealed last week the UK Culture Secretary has now officially tasked two UK regulators with probing the deal. The Love Island network is bullish that it will make it through the probe unscathed. “This is an expected and important milestone in the regulatory review process, and we are pleased that it is moving at pace,” said McCall. “We continue to expect completion in the second half of 2027.” The news was revealed today in ITV’s Q3 results, which showed total revenue of £2.7B, almost flat with the same figure for the first nine months of 2025. Media & Entertainment revenue was also virtually flat at £1.4B, with digital revenue helping offset the advertising declines. Producer-distributor ITV Studios , which is not being sold to Sky, also posted stable revenue of around £1.3B. Within ITV Studios, ITV said revenue, margin and profit are “heavily weighted to Q4,” pointing to a “strong pipeline of deliveries” like Netflix Italy’s SuburraMaxima, Peacock’s Love Island US: Beyond the Villa and the seventh season of Line of Duty for the BBC, alongside “significant high-margin licensing deals” in the global partnerships division. McCall said the sale of ITV network to Sky will “position ITV Studios as a highly attractive, pure play, global content business.” As previously guided, ITV Studios’ EBITA margin will be at the lower end of the 13% to 15% range, reflecting the revenue mix in the year, ITV said. Elsewhere, streaming hours to ITVX shot up by 29% to more than 2 billion minutes viewed. “Despite a more challenging market, we remain on track to deliver good revenue growth in ITV Studios and continued profitable digital revenue growth in Media & Entertainment (M&E) over the full year,” said McCall. “While the outlook for advertising remains muted, we are firmly focused on self help and mitigating actions, while continuing to execute our strategic priorities to drive performance across both businesses.” Sarandos Faces Unrest From Past & Present Execs Over Netflix’s Direction ‘Mike Hammer’ Star, Film & Stage Actor, Dies At 85; Career In Photos Jason Orley Directing New Take On Rom-Com ‘You’ve Got Mail’ For Warner Bros Leah McKendrick Sets ‘Voicemails From Isabelle’ Follow-Up; Maddie Ziegler Stars Read More About: Comments

title: ‘NAZA’ Becomes One Of The Most Watched Docs On Theatrical Release In 2026
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘NAZA’ Becomes One Of The Most Watched Docs On Theatrical Release In 2026 Tyler Gallant To Star In Caravaggio Art Heist Drama ‘Nativity’ Buyers Dig Beta Cinema’s Norwegian Oscar Entry ‘Growth Of The Soil’ View All November 11, 2026 1:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Filmmaker Yuval Abraham (right) interviews a source in 'NAZA' The Guardian/JW Films Bombshell Gaza documentary NAZA by Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor is on track to become one of the most-watched documentary films on theatrical release of 2026. New figures, collated by producers The Guardian and JW Films, reveal that the film had been seen by a world-wide audience of 1,547,033 across 47 territories by November 6. With $13.5 million in international gross, excluding the U.S. where it has grossed more than $1 million, it ranks among the best-performing documentaries internationally of 2026 to date. Related Stories News Avi Nesher's Israeli Box Office Hit 'Our Loves' Brings Its Characters "To The Brink" But Is Not An "October 7 Movie" News Asian World Film Festival Reveals Asian Vision & Focus On Sections Based on interviews with 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers, the documentary exposes the AI, phone surveillance and points-based systems deployed by the Israeli military in Gaza to identify targets, Hamas-related or otherwise, and then kill them in their homes regardless of whether other family members are likely to die in the strike as well. Watch on Deadline The documentary has performed best in Italy, where it was released by I Wonder on September 29 shortly after its Venice world premiere. The doc has reached 717.517 admissions there to date, with the film still playing in 379 cinemas, making history as the third most-watched documentary of all time in Italian cinemas, behind only Fahrenheit 9/11 and The March of the Penguins . Having started as a self-release through Michael Tuckman’s mTuckman Media in the U.S., Neon signed on as U.S. distributor in late October, aiming to enlarge the film’s footprint by building on the successful initial theatrical launch. To date the doc has clocked 83,673 admissions across the U.S. and Canada since its release on September 30. In the UK and Ireland, Dogwoof released NAZA on October 15 with a special live event screening at the Ritz in London, featuring directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, alongside producer Jim Wilson and exec producer Jonathan Glazer. The Q&A was broadcast live to a further 104 cinemas across the UK and Ireland. The release received strong support from the entire Picturehouse circuit, as well as venues from the three major multiplex chains (Odeon, Cineworld and Vue) alongside several independent cinemas. The live event alone attracted more than 7,000 admissions, with NAZA since climbing to 102.509 to date. In France, during a 48-hour event release due to French rules for films to be streamed online, NAZA attracted an audience of over 82,000 admissions. The film screened in more than 260 theaters nationwide, with nearly 500 screenings over two days. It topped the box office on both days, making it one of the most-watched documentaries in French theaters in 2026. The doc’s German distributor ImmerGuteFilme Germany has reported 83.355 admissions in the territory to date, with its strongest day to date on Sunday, November 1. In Austria , it has drawn 16.521 spectators, with Polyfilm releasing on October 1. In both countries, NAZA is outperforming Abraham and Szor’s Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land and Kaouther Ben Hania’s Oscar-nominated feature The Voice of Hind Rajab at the same stage. There was also a strong turnout in Spain, where Elastica released on October 9 on 105 screens, reaching 61.783 visitors by last Friday. Smaller countries are also reflecting the huge public interest in NAZA . Benelux distributor Cherry Pickers counted 132.323 admissions, a level of interest echoed by the over 50.000 visitors in Switzerland. The release said there are similar stories in other territories such as Australia / New Zealand, Scandinavia, Indonesia or Romania, Thailand, Poland, Mexico and Japan. The theatrical success follows the film’s high-profile premiere in Venice in September where it received a 25-minute ovation and won the Special Jury Prize. It has since won the Audience Award in San Sebastián and the Critics Prize at the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival. At the New York Critics Circle Awards on November 8, it won Best Political Documentary, having also been nominated for Best Documentary Feature and Best Directors. NAZA is nominated as Best Documentary Feature for the Gotham Film Awards and included in both the DOC NYC shortlist and the shortlist for Best European Documentary at the European Film Awards.
